But when, through a bad upbringing or bad company, the better part, which is also the smaller, is swamped by the larger mass of the worse, then we reproach the man and call him a slave to himself and undisciplined.'
'And rightly,' he said.

'Now look at our newly founded city,' I said, 'and you'll find one of these two conditions in it. You'll agree it can fairly be called master of itself, if a thing in which the better part rules the worse deserves to be called temperate and master of itself.'
'I'm looking,' he said, 'and what you say is true.'
'And the many complicated pleasures and pains and desires you'll find mostly in children and women and slaves, and in the great majority of so-called free men, the lowest sort.'
'Certainly.'
'While the simple, moderate desires, the ones guided by reasoning and by right belief and intelligence, you'll find in only a few, those born with the best natures and given the best education.'
'True.'
'And don't you see both of these in our city, with the desires of the worse and more numerous part held in check by the desires and the wisdom of the better and fewer?'
'I do,' he said.
'So if any city deserves to be called master of its own pleasures and desires, and master of itself, ours does.'
'It does indeed,' he said.
'And temperate too, for the same reasons?'
'Yes.'
'And if there's any city in which the rulers and the ruled agree about who should rule, it's ours.'
'Beyond a doubt.'
'And with the citizens in such agreement, in which group will temperance reside, the rulers or the ruled?'
'In both, I'd say,' he replied.
'You see we weren't far off,' I said, 'when we guessed temperance was a kind of harmony.'
'How do you mean?'

'Because, unlike courage and wisdom, each of which sat in one part of the city and made it brave or wise, temperance isn't like that. It stretches across the whole, making the weakest and the strongest and those in between all sing the same note, whether you rank them by intelligence, or strength, or numbers, or wealth, or anything else. So we'd be quite right to call temperance this agreement, this harmony between the naturally worse and the naturally better about which of them should rule, in a city or in a single man.'
'I agree completely,' he said.
'Good,' I said. 'So three of the four are in view in our city. What's the last kind, the one that makes a city good? Clearly it must be justice.'
'Clearly.'

'So now, Glaucon, like hunters, we have to surround the thicket and keep a sharp watch so justice doesn't slip away and vanish on us. She's in here somewhere, no doubt about it. So look hard, strain to catch sight of her, and if you spot her first, give me the word.'
'I wish I could,' he said. 'But really you should treat me as a follower, someone with just enough sight to make out whatever you point to. That's about all I'm good for.'
'Then say a prayer with me,' I said, 'and follow.'
'I will,' he said, 'only lead the way.'
'There's no path here,' I said, 'and the wood is dark and hard to see through. Still, we have to push on.'
'Then let's push on,' he said.
And just then I caught something. 'Look!' I cried. 'I think I see a track. I believe the quarry won't get away from us after all.'
'Good news,' he said.
'We really are slow-witted,' I said.
'How so?'

'My good man, it's been right under our feet from the start, ages ago, tumbling about there in front of us, and we never saw it. Nothing could be more absurd. It's like people hunting all over for something they're already holding in their hand. We kept staring off into the distance instead of at the thing in front of us, and that's probably how we missed it.'
'What do you mean?' he said.
'I mean that all this time, I think, we've been talking about justice and saying what it is without realizing that's what we were doing.'
'I'm getting impatient with this long preamble,' he said.

'Then tell me whether I'm right,' I said. 'You remember the principle we kept coming back to from the very founding of the city, that each man should do the one thing his nature best suits him for. Well, justice is that principle, or a part of it.'
'Yes, we kept saying each man should do one thing.'
'And we said, again and again, that justice is doing one's own work and not meddling in other people's. Plenty of others have said the same.'
'We did say that.'
'Then it seems, my friend, that doing one's own work, in a certain way, is justice. Do you know what makes me think so?'
'No, tell me.'

'I think it's because this is the one thing left over in the city once we've set aside the others we examined, temperance, courage, and wisdom. It's what made all of those possible in the first place, and once they're there it keeps them safe as long as it stays in them. And we did say that if we found the other three, justice would be the one remaining.'
'That follows of necessity,' he said.

'Now, if we had to decide which of these four does most, by being present, to make the city good, it wouldn't be easy. Is it the agreement of rulers and ruled? Or the soldiers' preservation of the lawful belief about what's truly to be feared? Or the wisdom and watchfulness in the rulers? Or is it this other thing, present in child and woman, slave and free, craftsman, ruler, and ruled, the doing of one's own single work and not meddling? Which deserves the prize? It's hard to say.'
'It is,' he said.
'So this power, each man in the city doing his own work, seems to compete with the other three virtues, wisdom and temperance and courage, for making the city good.'
'It does,' he said.
'And we'd call this competing virtue justice?'
'Exactly.'
'Look at it another way, and see if you agree. Won't you assign your rulers the job of judging lawsuits?'
'Of course.'
'And when they judge, what will they aim at but this, that no one take what belongs to another or be deprived of his own?'
'Yes, that's the principle.'
'Because that's just?'
'Yes.'
'So on this view too, justice turns out to be the having and doing of what is one's own and belongs to one.'
'That's right.'

'Now see whether you agree with this. Suppose a carpenter set about doing the shoemaker's work, or the shoemaker the carpenter's, and they swapped their tools and their jobs, or suppose one man tried to do both at once. Would the city take much harm from that?'
'Not much,' he said.

'But suppose a man who's a craftsman by nature, or some other money-maker, gets puffed up by his wealth or his strength or the number of his supporters, and tries to force his way into the soldier class, or a soldier into the class of the rulers and guardians when he isn't fit for it, and they trade their tools and their jobs around; or suppose one man tries to do all of these at once. I think you'll agree that this swapping and meddling among the three classes is the ruin of the city.'
'Absolutely.'
'So the meddling and exchange among these three classes is the greatest harm to the city, and we'd be most justified in calling it the worst of crimes against it.'
'Just so.'
'And the worst crime against one's own city, wouldn't you call that injustice?'
'Of course.'
'So this is injustice. And turn it around: when the money-making class, the soldiers, and the guardians each do their own work in the city, that is justice, and it makes the city just.'
'I'd say that's exactly so,' he said.

'Let's not be too sure just yet,' I said. 'If this idea of justice holds good when we apply it to the individual man as well as the city, we'll grant it; there'll be nothing more to say. But if it doesn't fit the individual, we'll have to look again. First, let's finish what we set out to do. We took it that if we examined justice on the larger scale first, in something bigger that has it, we'd find it easier to make out in the single man. The city seemed to be that larger thing, so we built the best one we could, sure that justice would be found in a good city. Now let's carry over what we found there to the individual. If it matches, good. If the individual shows us something different, we'll go back to the city and test the idea again. Maybe, by rubbing the two cases together like fire-sticks, we'll make justice flash out, and once we've seen it we can fix it firmly in our minds.'
'That's the right way to go about it,' he said. 'Let's do as you say.'
'Now,' I said, 'when you call two things by the same name, one larger and one smaller, are they alike or unlike in respect of the thing the name refers to?'
'Alike,' he said.
'So the just man, in respect of justice itself, won't differ at all from the just city; he'll be like it.'
'He will,' he said.

'And we decided a city is just when each of its three kinds of nature does its own work, and that it's temperate and brave and wise because of certain other conditions and states of those same three.'
'True.'
'So we'll expect the individual to have these same three kinds in his soul, and to deserve the same names as the city because he's in the same conditions as it is.'
'That must be so,' he said.
'Once again, then, my friend, we've stumbled into an easy little question about the soul, whether it has these three kinds in it or not.'
'It doesn't look so easy to me,' he said. 'But maybe the proverb's right, Socrates, that fine things are hard.'

'Apparently,' I said. 'And I'll tell you frankly, Glaucon, that in my opinion we'll never get a precise answer to this by the methods we've been using. The road that leads there is another and a longer one. Still, we may reach an answer that's up to the standard of what we've already said.'
'Won't that do?' he said. 'For now it would satisfy me.'
'And me,' I said.
'Then don't give up,' he said. 'Press on with the inquiry.'

'Well,' I said, 'we have to admit, don't we, that each of us has in himself the very same kinds and characters that are in the city? Where else could the city have got them from? It would be absurd to think that the spirited, high-tempered quality came to be in a city from any source but the individuals who have it, the people we credit with it, the Thracians and Scythians and the northern peoples generally. Or take the love of learning, which one might especially credit to our part of the world, or the love of money, which you could fairly attribute to the Phoenicians and the Egyptians.'
'Exactly,' he said.
'So this much is plain enough,' I said.
'Quite plain.'

'But here's where it gets harder. Do we do each of these with the same part of ourselves, or with three different parts? Do we learn with one part, get angry with another, and with a third desire the pleasures of food and sex and the like, or do we do each of these with the whole soul? That's what's hard to settle.'
'I agree,' he said. 'That's the difficulty.'
'Then let's try this way to decide whether they're the same or different.'
'How?' he asked.

'It's clear,' I said, 'that the same thing can't do or undergo opposite things in the same respect and in relation to the same thing at the same time. So if we find that happening here, we'll know we're dealing not with one thing but with more than one.'
'All right.'
'Take this case. Can the same thing be at rest and in motion at the same time, in the same part of itself?'
'Of course not.'

'Let's be even more precise, so we don't fall out over words later. If someone said of a man who's standing still but moving his hands and his head that the same man is both at rest and in motion at once, we wouldn't accept that way of speaking. We'd say one part of him is at rest and another in motion.'
'True.'

'And if our objector got cleverer still and pointed out that a spinning top, whirling with its point fixed in one spot, is at rest and in motion as a whole at the same time, and said the same of anything that turns in place, we wouldn't accept it, because such things aren't at rest and in motion in the same part of themselves. We'd say they have an axis and a circumference; with respect to the axis they're at rest, since they don't lean off it, and with respect to the circumference they're moving. But if the axis itself tips to the right or left, forward or back, while it spins, then it's not at rest in any respect.'
'And we'd be right to say so,' he replied.
'So no objection of that kind will throw us off or persuade us that one and the same thing could ever, in the same respect and toward the same thing, at the same time, do or undergo opposites.'
'It won't, not as far as I'm concerned,' he said.

'Still,' I said, 'so we don't have to wade through every such objection and prove each one false, let's assume this principle is sound and go ahead, agreeing that if it ever turns out to be false, everything we build on it falls with it.'
'That's the best way,' he said.

'Now then,' I said, 'wouldn't you put nodding yes and shaking the head no, reaching for something and pushing it away, drawing toward and thrusting off, all in the class of opposites, whether they're things you do or things done to you? That makes no difference to their being opposites.'
'Yes,' he said, 'they're opposites.'

'And what about thirst and hunger, and the desires generally, and willing and wishing? Wouldn't you put all of those somewhere among the things we just mentioned? Wouldn't you say the soul of a man who desires is reaching for the thing it desires, drawing toward itself what it wants to have, or that, insofar as it wills something to be given to it, it nods yes to itself, longing for that, as if someone had asked it a question?'
'I would.'
'And not-willing, refusing, not desiring, wouldn't we put those with the soul's pushing away and thrusting off, the opposite class?'
'Of course.'
'That being so, let's say there's a class of desires, and the clearest of them are the ones we call thirst and hunger.'
'Let's say so,' he said.
'And one of these is for drink, the other for food?'
'Yes.'

'Now, insofar as it's thirst, is it a desire in the soul for anything more than what we said, for drink? Is thirst, just as thirst, a thirst for hot drink or cold, for much or little, for any particular kind of drink at all? Or is it that if heat goes along with the thirst, that adds the desire for something cold, and if cold, for something hot; and if the thirst is great because of some added largeness, the desire is for much, and if small, for little? But thirst itself will never be a desire for anything but its natural object, drink, just as hunger is for food.'
'That's right,' he said. 'Each desire, in itself, is just for its own natural object, and the desire for a particular kind of thing comes from something added on.'

'Let's be careful here,' I said, 'so that no one catches us off guard with the objection that no one desires drink as such, but good drink, or food as such, but good food, since everyone desires good things, and so, thirst being a desire, it must be a desire for good drink, and the same with every other desire.'
'There might be something to that objection,' he said.

'But surely,' I said, 'with things that are relative to something, the qualified ones are relative to a qualified object, while the thing taken by itself is relative only to its object taken by itself.'
'I don't follow,' he said.
'You understand that the greater is what it is in relation to the less?'
'Certainly.'
'And the much greater to the much less?'
'Yes.'
'And the once-greater to the once-less, and the going-to-be-greater to the going-to-be-less?'
'Of course,' he said.
'And so with more in relation to fewer, double to half, and all such pairs, and heavier to lighter, faster to slower, and again hot to cold, and everything of that kind?'
'Yes.'

'And isn't it the same with the branches of knowledge? Knowledge as such is knowledge of what can be learned, or whatever we should call its object, while a particular knowledge of a particular kind is knowledge of a particular object. Take the building of houses: it's a kind of knowledge, marked off from the others, and so it's called architecture.'
'Certainly.'
'And it's called that because it has a particular character that none of the others has?'
'Yes.'
'And it has that character because it has an object of a particular kind, and the same goes for all the other arts and branches of knowledge?'
'It does.'

'Well then,' I said, 'take that as what I meant before about relatives, if you understand me now. I meant that whenever one term is taken just by itself, it's relative to its object just by itself, and whenever it's qualified, to a qualified object. I'm not saying it's relative to an object of its own kind, that knowledge of health is itself healthy or knowledge of disease diseased, or that knowledge of good and bad is itself good or bad. I'm only saying that once knowledge becomes knowledge not of its object as such but of a qualified object, in this case of health and disease, it gets a particular character itself, and so it's no longer called just knowledge but, with the qualification added, medicine.'
'I understand,' he said, 'and I think you're right.'
'And thirst, won't you put it among the things that are relative to something, being what it is in relation to something?'
'I will,' he said. 'Thirst is relative to drink.'
'So a particular kind of thirst is for a particular kind of drink, but thirst itself isn't for much or little, good or bad, or any particular kind of drink at all, but simply for drink itself.'
'Absolutely.'
'So the soul of the thirsty man, insofar as he's thirsty, wants nothing but to drink. That's what it reaches for and strains toward.'
'Plainly.'

'Then if something ever pulls it back when it's thirsty, that must be something in it different from the thirsty part, the part that drives it like a beast to drink. For we agreed the same thing can't, with the same part of itself, at the same time, in relation to the same object, do opposite things.'
'No, it can't.'
'Just as you wouldn't say the archer's hands push the bow away and draw it in at the same time, but that one hand pushes and the other pulls.'
'Exactly,' he said.
'Now, can a man be thirsty and yet unwilling to drink?'
'Yes,' he said, 'that happens all the time.'
'And what should we say about that? Isn't there something in his soul telling him to drink, and something else, different, holding him back, something that overrules the part that's telling him to?'
'I think so,' he said.
'And doesn't the part that holds him back, when it holds him back, come from reasoning, while the part that drives and drags him comes from feelings and from disorders of the body?'
'It seems so.'

'So we'd be right to judge them two distinct things,' I said. 'The part of the soul by which it reasons we'll call the rational part; the part by which it lusts and hungers and thirsts and is stirred by the other desires, the irrational and appetitive part, the companion of certain satisfactions and pleasures.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's a fair way to think of it.'

'Then let's take it as settled that these two parts exist in the soul. Now, what about the spirited part, the part by which we feel anger? Is it a third, or is it the same in nature as one of these two?'
'It might be the same as the appetitive part,' he said.

'There's a story I once heard,' I said, 'and I believe it. Leontius, the son of Aglaion, was coming up from the Piraeus, along the outside of the north wall, when he saw the public executioner's corpses lying there. He wanted to look at them and at the same time was disgusted and turned himself away. For a while he fought with himself and covered his eyes, but in the end his desire got the better of him, and he ran over to the bodies, forcing his eyes wide open and crying, "There, curse you, feast yourselves on the lovely sight!"'
'I've heard that story too,' he said.
'And its point,' I said, 'is that anger sometimes makes war on the desires, as though it were one thing and they were another.'
'That is the point,' he said.

'And don't we notice, in plenty of other cases, that when a man's desires force him against his reasoning, he rails at himself and his anger rises against the part of him that's forcing him? It's as if there were two factions at war, and his spirit takes the side of his reason. But when his spirit sides with the desires against what reason has decided shouldn't be done, that's a thing I think you've never noticed happening in yourself, or, I'd guess, in anyone else.'
'No, never,' he said.

'And take a man who believes he's done wrong. The finer his nature, the less he's able to feel anger when he suffers hunger or cold or any other pain at the hands of the man he wronged, because he thinks it's deserved. His spirit, as I say, refuses to rouse itself against it.'
'True,' he said.

'But when a man believes he's the one being wronged, then his spirit boils and rages and fights on the side of what he takes to be just. Through hunger and cold and every other suffering it holds out and wins, and his noble spirit won't be quieted until it has either won through or died, or until, like a dog called off by its shepherd, it is called back and calmed by the reason within him.'
'A perfect comparison,' he said. 'And it fits what we said about our city, that the auxiliaries were to be like dogs, obeying the rulers, who are like the shepherds of the city.'
'You understand me exactly,' I said. 'But there's one more thing to consider.'
'What's that?'

'That the spirited part has turned out to be the opposite of what we just thought. We supposed it was a kind of desire, but now we say that, in the soul's civil war, it takes up arms on the side of reason.'
'Definitely,' he said.

'But is it then different from reason as well, or only a kind of reason? In that case there wouldn't be three parts of the soul but two, the rational and the appetitive. Or just as the city was held together by three classes, the money-makers, the auxiliaries, and the rulers, is there in the soul too this third thing, the spirited part, the natural helper of reason, as long as it hasn't been ruined by a bad upbringing?'
'There must be a third,' he said.
'Yes,' I said, 'provided it turns out to be distinct from reason, just as we showed it was distinct from desire.'

'That's easy to show,' he said. 'You can see it in small children. They're full of spirit from the moment they're born, while some of them, in my view, never come to reason at all, and most do so only late.'

'A fine point,' I said. 'And you can see the same in animals, which is further proof of what you say. And we can call again on the line of Homer we quoted before, where he says, "He struck his breast and rebuked his heart." There Homer clearly treats the part that reasons about better and worse as different from the part that feels unreasoning anger and is rebuked by it.'
'Exactly right,' he said.
'So,' I said, 'after a hard swim we've reached land, and we're fairly agreed that the same three kinds are in the soul that are in the city.'
'Just so.'
'Then doesn't it follow at once that the individual is wise in the same way and by the same part that makes the city wise?'
'Certainly.'
'And that the part that makes the individual brave is the same that makes the city brave, and so on, the individual matching the city in every virtue?'
'It must be so.'
'And we'll say a man is just, Glaucon, in the same way the city is just.'
'That follows too, of course.'
'And we haven't forgotten that the city was just because each of its three classes did its own work?'
'I don't think we've forgotten,' he said.
'Then we must keep in mind that each of us, too, will be just, and do his own work, when each of the parts in him does its own.'
'Yes,' he said, 'we must keep that in mind.'
'And isn't it for the rational part, since it is wise and looks after the whole soul, to rule, and for the spirited part to be its subject and its ally?'
'Certainly.'

'And, as we said, won't the blend of music and physical training bring these two into accord, tightening and feeding the reason with fine words and learning, and loosening, soothing, and taming the spirited part with harmony and rhythm?'
'Just so,' he said.

'And these two, so nourished and truly taught their own work, will govern the appetitive part, which in each of us is the largest part of the soul and by nature the greediest for money. They'll watch it closely, in case it grows fat and strong on the so-called pleasures of the body and stops keeping to its own work, and tries instead to enslave and rule the parts it has no business ruling, and so wrecks the whole life of the man.'
'Quite so,' he said.

'And wouldn't these two be the best guardians of the whole soul and the whole body against enemies from outside, the one taking counsel, the other doing battle, following its ruler and carrying out by its courage what reason decides?'
'Yes.'
'And we call a man brave, I think, when his spirited part holds onto what reason declares is and isn't to be feared, through pleasure and through pain alike.'
'Rightly,' he said.

'And we call him wise by that small part of him that rules and gives those declarations, the part that has in it the knowledge of what's good for each of the three parts and for the whole they make together.'
'Certainly.'
'And don't we call him temperate by the friendship and harmony of these same parts, when the ruler and the two ruled agree that the rational part should rule and don't make war on it?'
'That's exactly what temperance is,' he said, 'in a city or in a man.'
'And of course a man will be just by what we've now said so many times, and in the way we've said.'
'Necessarily.'
'Now,' I said, 'is justice in the individual any blurrier than it was in the city? Does it come out as something different there, or the same?'
'The same, I'd say,' he replied.
'Because, if any doubt is still hanging in our minds, we can settle it for certain with a few ordinary examples.'
'What sort of examples?'

'Suppose someone asked us about that just city and a man brought up in its spirit, whether such a man would embezzle a deposit of gold or silver entrusted to him. Who would think he'd be more likely to do it than men of the other sort?'
'No one,' he said.
'And wouldn't such a man be the last to commit temple-robbery, or theft, or betrayal, whether of his friends in private or of his city in public?'
'He would.'
'And he'd never be faithless to an oath or any other agreement?'
'How could he?'
'And adultery, neglect of his parents, failure in his religious duties, no one would be less likely to fall into any of these than he.'
'No one,' he said.
'And isn't the reason for all this that each part of him is doing its own work, in ruling and in being ruled?'
'Yes, exactly that, and nothing else.'
'Then are you still looking for justice to be something other than this power that produces such men and such cities?'
'No, by Zeus, I'm not,' he said.

'So our dream has come true. The hunch we had at the very start of building the city, that by some god's help we'd hit from the beginning on a kind of origin and pattern of justice, has now been borne out.'
'It certainly has.'
'So the principle that the carpenter and the shoemaker and the rest should each do their own work and not another's, that was a kind of image of justice, which is why it was useful.'
'Plainly.'

'But in truth justice was something of this sort, only it isn't concerned with a man's outward doings but with what's inside him, with his true self and what truly belongs to him. The just man doesn't let any part of his soul do another part's work, or meddle with the others. He sets his own house in order, takes command of himself, brings himself into tune, and becomes a friend to himself. He binds together the three parts, like the three fixed notes of a scale, the highest and the lowest and the one between, and any others there may be in between those, and from being many he becomes entirely one, temperate and in harmony. Only then does he act, whether in getting and spending, or in caring for his body, or in some matter of politics or private dealing, and through it all he believes and calls just and fine any action that preserves this inner harmony and helps produce it, and the knowledge that oversees such action he calls wisdom. And he calls unjust any action that breaks this harmony down, and the belief that oversees that, ignorance.'
'That is the exact truth, Socrates,' he said.
'Good,' I said. 'So if we claimed to have found the just man and the just city, and what justice is in each, I don't think we'd be lying.'
'We certainly wouldn't.'
'Shall we say it, then?'
'Let's say it.'
'So be it,' I said. 'And now we have to look at injustice.'
'Plainly.'

'Won't it have to be a kind of civil war among the three parts, a meddling and interfering in one another's work, a rising up of one part of the soul against the whole to seize a rule that isn't its by right, the rule of a part whose nature is to be a subject of the part that ought to rule? Disorder and confusion of that kind, I think, is what we'll call injustice, along with license and cowardice and ignorance, in a word, every form of vice.'
'Exactly so,' he said.
'Then if we know clearly what injustice and justice are, we also know clearly, don't we, what acting unjustly and being unjust come to, and likewise acting justly?'
'How do you mean?' he said.
'They're just like the healthy and the unhealthy,' I said. 'What health and disease are in the body, justice and injustice are in the soul.'
'How so?' he said.
'Healthy things produce health, and unhealthy things produce disease.'
'Yes.'
'And just actions produce justice, unjust actions injustice?'
'They must.'

'And producing health means setting up among the parts of the body a natural order, in which one rules and another is ruled, while producing disease means setting up an order against nature, in which one part rules and another is ruled contrary to nature?'
'True.'
'And isn't producing justice the same, setting up among the parts of the soul a natural order of ruling and being ruled, while producing injustice means an order against nature?'
'Exactly so,' he said.
'So virtue, it seems, is a kind of health and beauty and good condition of the soul, and vice a disease and ugliness and weakness of it.'
'That's right.'
'And don't fine practices lead to virtue, and shameful ones to vice?'
'They must.'

'So now, it seems, all that's left is to ask which pays better, to do what's just, to follow fine practices and be just, whether anyone notices or not, or to do what's unjust and be unjust, provided one isn't punished and so forced to improve.'

'But Socrates,' he said, 'to me that question has become ridiculous. When the body's nature is ruined, we think life isn't worth living, even with all the food and drink and wealth and power in the world. So when the very nature of the thing by which we live is disordered and ruined, are we really going to say life is worth living, as long as a man can do whatever he likes, except the one thing that would free him from vice and injustice and win him justice and virtue, now that we've seen what each of them is?'
'Yes, the question is ridiculous,' I said. 'But still, now that we've come to the point where we can see the truth of all this as clearly as anything, we mustn't give up.'
'No,' he said, 'least of all now.'
'Then come up here,' I said, 'and look down at how many forms vice has, the ones worth looking at, at any rate.'
'I'm right behind you,' he said. 'Go on.'

'From the height the argument has climbed to,' I said, 'it's like standing on a watchtower. From here you can see that virtue is one, but the forms of vice are countless, though four of them are worth singling out.'
'What do you mean?' he said.
'I mean,' I said, 'that there seem to be as many types of soul as there are distinct types of city worth naming.'
'How many is that?'
'Five kinds of city,' I said, 'and five of soul.'
'And what are they?' he asked.

'The first kind of city,' I said, 'is the one we've been describing, and it could go by either of two names. Where one outstanding man rules, you'd call it a monarchy; where several rule, an aristocracy.'
'True,' he said.
'But I count these as a single form. Whether the rulers are one or many, as long as they've been brought up and educated the way we've laid down, they won't disturb the city's fundamental laws.'
'No, they won't,' he said.

So this is the kind of city and the kind of man I call good and right; and if this one is right, then every other is wrong. The badness is one thing, but it shows up in the running of a state and in the ordering of a single soul alike, and it takes four different forms.
'And what are those?' he asked.

I was about to lay out the order in which these four bad forms seemed to me to arise out of one another, when Polemarchus, who was sitting a little way off, just beyond Adeimantus, reached out, took hold of Adeimantus's cloak up by the shoulder, and pulled him close. Leaning in, he whispered something in his ear. I caught only the words, 'Shall we let him off, or what do we do?'
'Absolutely not,' said Adeimantus, this time out loud.
'Let whom off?' I asked. 'Who is it you won't release?'
'You,' he said.
'And why me especially?' I asked.

'Because,' he said, 'we think you're being lazy. You mean to cheat us out of a whole stretch of the argument, an important one, and you imagine we won't notice you skating past it, as though it were obvious to everyone that, where women and children are concerned, friends hold everything in common.'
'But isn't that right, Adeimantus?' I said.

'Yes,' he said, 'but "right" here, like everything else, needs explaining. There's more than one way to hold things in common, so tell us which one you mean. We've been waiting a long time for you to say something about how your citizens will have children, and how they'll raise them once they're born, and in general what this whole business of holding women and children in common amounts to. We think the way these things are handled, well or badly, makes an enormous difference to a state, for better or for worse. And now, just as you're starting up another city instead, we've decided, as you heard, not to let you go until you've given a full account of all this.'
'You can count me in on that resolution,' said Glaucon.
'And without further ado,' said Thrasymachus, 'take it that we're all of one mind about it.'

'You don't realize what you're doing, ganging up on me like this,' I said. 'What an argument you're stirring up about the state! Just when I thought I was finished and was glad to have gotten that question to lie down quietly, congratulating myself that you'd accepted what I said, you make me start over from the very foundations. You have no idea what a hornet's nest of words you're poking. I saw this trouble coming, which is exactly why I steered around it.'
'What do you think we came here for,' said Thrasymachus, 'to dig for gold, or to hear a discussion?'
'To hear a discussion,' I said, 'but within reason.'

'Socrates,' said Glaucon, 'a sensible man sets no limit on hearing this kind of discussion short of his whole life. But never mind us. Don't lose heart on our account. Just answer the question your own way: what is this community of women and children that's to hold among our guardians? And how will we handle the stretch between birth and the start of education, which seems to call for the most care of all? Tell us how these things are to go.'

'It isn't an easy thing to explain, my friend,' I said. 'There's even more room for doubt here than in what we settled before. People will question whether what I'm proposing is even possible; and even granting it could be done, they'll still doubt whether it would be for the best. That's why I hold back from the subject, afraid the whole idea may turn out to be nothing but a daydream.'
'Don't be afraid,' he said. 'Your listeners won't be hard on you. We're not skeptics, and we're not hostile.'
'My good friend,' I said, 'I suppose you say that to encourage me.'
'I do,' he said.

'Then you're doing the opposite,' I said. 'Your encouragement would be fine if I were sure I knew what I was talking about. A man who knows the truth about things he cares about and holds dear can speak it among wise friends who love him with no fear and no faltering. But to push ahead with an argument while you're still a hesitant, searching man yourself, which is my condition, that's a dangerous, slippery business. Not because I'd be laughed at, that fear would be childish, but because I might miss the truth on the very questions where I most need to keep my footing, and drag my friends down with me in the fall. So I pray to Nemesis to forgive what I'm about to say. For I honestly believe it's a lesser crime to kill a man by accident than to deceive people about what is fine, or good, or just, especially when laws are at stake. That's a risk I'd rather run among enemies than among friends, so your encouragement does me no favors.'
Glaucon laughed. 'Well then, Socrates,' he said, 'if your argument does us any harm, we acquit you in advance, as if of manslaughter. You won't be charged with deceiving us. So take heart and speak.'
'Fine,' I said. 'The law does say that a man acquitted is free of guilt, and if it holds in court it ought to hold in argument too.'
'Then speak,' he said, 'and don't hold back.'

'Well,' I said, 'I'll have to go back and pick up what I probably should have said earlier, in its proper place. Perhaps it's fitting this way: the men have played their part, and now it's the women's turn. I'll speak of them, all the more gladly since you've asked.'

'For men born and raised as our citizens are, the only right way I can see to settle how women and children are to be had and handled is to follow the path we set out on at the start, when we said the men were to be guardians, watchdogs of the flock.'
'True.'
'Then let's go on and assume that the birth and upbringing of our women follow the same rules, or nearly the same, and see whether the result fits our design.'
'What do you mean?'

'Let me put it as a question,' I said. 'When it comes to dogs, do we split them into males and females, or do both share equally in hunting and standing guard and the other work of dogs? Do we hand the whole care of the flock over to the males alone, and leave the females at home on the grounds that bearing and nursing the pups is work enough for them?'
'No,' he said, 'they share the work alike. The only difference is that the males are stronger and the females weaker.'
'And can you use any animal for the same work as another unless you raise and feed it the same way?'
'You can't.'
'So if women are to do the same work as men, they have to be given the same upbringing and the same education?'
'Yes.'
'Now the education we gave the men was music and physical training.'
'Yes.'
'Then we'll have to give women music and physical training too, and train them in war as well, and put them to the same use as the men.'
'That follows, I suppose.'
'I expect,' I said, 'that quite a few of our proposals, just because they break with custom, will look ridiculous if they're actually carried out.'
'No doubt of it.'

'And what will look most ridiculous of all? The sight of women exercising naked alongside the men in the gymnasium, especially the older ones. They'll hardly be a vision of beauty, any more than the eager old men who keep showing up at the gym in spite of their wrinkles and their looks.'
'Yes,' he said, 'by today's standards that would seem absurd.'

'But since we've made up our minds to speak plainly,' I said, 'we mustn't be frightened off by the jokes the clever wits will make at this kind of innovation, all the things they'll say about women in the gym and the music room, and above all about women in armor, riding horses.'
'Very true,' he said.

'But having started, we have to push on over the rough ground of the law, and just for once ask these gentlemen to be serious. We can remind them that not so long ago the Greeks themselves thought, as most foreigners still think, that the sight of a naked man was ridiculous and shameful. When the Cretans first, and then the Spartans, took up the practice of exercising naked, the wits of that day could have mocked it just the same.'
'No doubt.'

'But once experience showed it was better to strip than to keep everything covered up, the eye's first sense of the absurd faded before the better principle that reason laid down. And it became clear that the real fool is the man who aims his ridicule at anything other than folly and vice, or who seriously tries to measure beauty by any standard but the good.'
'Very true,' he said.

'So first, whether we put the question in jest or in earnest, let's come to an understanding about woman's nature. Is she capable of sharing in all of man's work, or only part of it, or none? And is war one of the things she can share in, or not? That's the best way to begin the inquiry, and it'll probably bring us to the fairest conclusion.'
'By far the best way.'
'Shall we argue the other side ourselves, then, and make the case against our own position? That way the opposing view won't go undefended.'
'Why not?' he said.

'Then let's put a speech in our opponents' mouths. They'll say: "Socrates, Glaucon, no outsider needs to refute you. You did it yourselves. Right at the founding of the state you agreed that each person should do the one job that suits his nature." And we did agree to that, if I'm not mistaken. "And don't the natures of men and women differ a great deal?" Of course they do, we'll say. "Then shouldn't the work given to men and to women differ too, each suited to their different natures?" Certainly. "But then, haven't you fallen into a flat contradiction, saying that men and women, whose natures are so completely different, ought to do the very same things?" Now, my friend, what defense will you make for us against an objection like that?'
'That's not an easy thing to answer on the spot,' he said. 'So I ask you, and I'm asking in earnest, to make the case for our side yourself.'

'These are the objections, Glaucon,' I said, 'and many others like them, that I saw coming long ago. They're what made me afraid and reluctant to lay down any law about the having and raising of women and children.'
'By Zeus,' he said, 'this is anything but easy to solve.'
'It isn't,' I said. 'But the fact is, when a man falls into the water, whether it's a little swimming pool or the open sea, he has to swim all the same.'
'Very true.'
'So we have to swim too, and try to reach the shore, hoping that some dolphin of Arion's or some other piece of luck will carry us across.'
'I suppose so,' he said.

'Then let's see if we can find a way out. We agreed, didn't we, that different natures should have different pursuits, and that the natures of men and women differ. And yet now we're saying that these different natures should have the same pursuits. That's the inconsistency we're charged with.'
'Exactly.'
'Glaucon,' I said, 'what a glorious power there is in the art of contradiction!'
'Why do you say that?'

'Because I think plenty of people fall into it without meaning to. They think they're reasoning when really they're just quarreling over words, because they can't carve up a subject and look at it part by part. So they go after a merely verbal disagreement, in a competitive spirit rather than a fair one.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that does happen often. But what's it got to do with us, right now?'
'A great deal,' I said, 'because there's a real danger we've slipped into a verbal dispute without realizing it.'
'How so?'

'We've been bravely and stubbornly insisting on the bare verbal point that different natures shouldn't have the same pursuits. But we never stopped to ask what we even meant by sameness or difference of nature, or in what respect we were distinguishing them when we assigned different work to different natures and the same work to the same.'
'No,' he said, 'we never looked into that.'

'Then take this for an example,' I said. 'Suppose we asked whether bald men and long-haired men have opposite natures. And once we'd agreed they do, then if bald men were shoemakers we'd have to forbid the long-haired ones to make shoes, and the other way around.'
'That would be a joke,' he said.

'Yes, a joke,' I said. 'And why? Because when we built the state we never meant that opposite natures should differ in every way, only in the ways that bear on the particular work in question. We'd have said, for instance, that a man with a doctor's soul and a man who actually is a doctor have the same nature.'
'True.'
'Whereas a doctor and a carpenter have different natures?'
'Of course.'

'So,' I said, 'if the male and female sex turn out to differ with respect to some art or pursuit, then we'd say that pursuit ought to be assigned to one or the other. But if the only difference is that the female bears children and the male begets them, that's no proof at all that a woman differs from a man in the way that matters for the education she should get. So we'll go on maintaining that our guardians and their women should have the same pursuits.'
'And rightly so,' he said.
'Next, we'll ask our opponent to name a single one of the arts or pursuits of civic life in which a woman's nature differs from a man's.'
'That's a fair challenge.'
'And maybe he'll say, as you did, that it isn't easy to answer on the spot, but with a little thought it's no great difficulty.'
'He might.'

'Then suppose we invite the man who raises this objection to walk through the argument with us. Maybe we can show him there's nothing in the makeup of a woman that bears specially on running a state.'
'By all means.'

'Let's say to him: come now, answer us this. When you spoke of one man being gifted by nature for something and another not, didn't you mean this, that one man picks a thing up easily and another with difficulty; that a little instruction sets one of them discovering a great deal on his own, while the other, after much study and effort, can't even hold on to what he learns; that the body of the one serves his mind well, while the body of the other gets in his way? Aren't these the sorts of things that mark off the naturally gifted from the ungifted?'
'No one would deny it.'

'And is there any human pursuit in which men, as a sex, don't surpass women in all these respects? Need I waste time on weaving, and the management of pancakes and preserves, the things women really do seem to shine at, where to be beaten by a man would be the most absurd thing of all?'
'You're right,' he said, 'that on the whole one sex is far outdone by the other. Many women, to be sure, are better than many men at many things, but taken altogether it's as you say.'

'Then, my friend,' I said, 'there's no occupation in running a state that belongs to a woman because she's a woman, or to a man because he's a man. The natural gifts are scattered alike through both. By nature a woman has a share in every pursuit, and so does a man, though in all of them a woman is the weaker.'
'Quite true.'
'Then are we to lay all the work on men and none on women?'
'That would never do.'
'No, because one woman has a gift for medicine and another doesn't; one is musical by nature and another isn't.'
'Certainly.'
'And one woman has a turn for athletics and war, while another has no fight in her and no taste for the gym?'
'No doubt.'
'And one woman loves wisdom and another hates it; one has spirit and another has none?'
'That's true as well.'
'So one woman has the temperament of a guardian and another doesn't. Wasn't it just this sort of nature we looked for when we picked out the male guardians?'
'It was.'
'Then men and women have the same nature when it comes to guarding the state. They differ only in being stronger or weaker.'
'So it seems.'
'And the women with the right qualities are to be chosen to live and work alongside the men who have them, since they're alike in ability and alike in character?'
'Certainly.'
'And the same natures should have the same pursuits?'
'They should.'
'Then we've come back around to where we were: there's nothing unnatural in giving the guardians' women the same music and physical training as the men.'
'Nothing at all.'
'So the law we laid down was in accord with nature, not impossible and not a mere wish. It's the contrary practice, the one in force now, that turns out to go against nature.'
'It looks that way.'
'Now, we set out to ask two things: first, whether our proposals were possible, and second, whether they were for the best.'
'We did.'
'And we've agreed they're possible?'
'Yes.'
'Then the next thing is to settle that they're also greatly beneficial?'
'Clearly.'
'You'll grant that the same education that makes a man a good guardian will make a woman one too, since their underlying nature is the same?'
'Yes.'
'Then let me ask you something.'
'Go ahead.'
'Would you say all men are equal in excellence, or that one man is better than another?'
'That one is better than another.'
'And in the city we're founding, who do you suppose come out the better men, the guardians who've had the upbringing we described, or the shoemakers whose education has been in shoemaking?'
'What a ridiculous question.'
'I take your point,' I said. 'And aren't the guardians the best of our citizens?'
'By far.'
'And won't their women be the best of the women?'
'By far, yes.'
'And can anything be better for a state than that its men and its women should be as good as they can possibly be?'
'Nothing.'
'And that's exactly what music and physical training will bring about, present in the way we've laid out?'
'Of course.'
'So the law we've enacted is not only possible but as beneficial to the state as anything could be.'
'It is.'

'Then let the guardians' women strip for exercise, since their excellence will be their clothing, and let them share in war and in the defense of the country. Only in dividing up the work, the lighter tasks should go to the women, because they're the weaker, but otherwise their duties are the same. And as for the man who laughs at the sight of women exercising naked for the best of reasons, he's a man harvesting',
'"the unripe fruit of his own wit,"',
'and he has no idea what he's laughing at or what he's doing. For it always has been, and always will be, the best of sayings: what's useful is fine, and what's harmful is shameful.'
'Very true.'

'So here's one wave in our law about women that we can say we've now ridden out. It hasn't swallowed us alive for laying down that the guardians, men and women alike, should share all their pursuits. The argument's own consistency bears witness both that the thing is useful and that it's possible.'
'Yes, that was a mighty wave you've gotten past.'
'And you'll think it was nothing,' I said, 'once you see the one that's coming.'
'Go on, then. Let me see it.'

'The law that follows from this one, and from everything before it, runs like this: that these women are all to be shared in common among these men, and none is to live privately with any man; and the children too are to be shared in common, and no parent is to know his own child, nor any child his parent.'
'That,' he said, 'is a far bigger wave than the other. There'll be much more doubt both about whether it could be done and about whether it would do any good.'

'As to its doing good,' I said, 'I don't think there can be much dispute that having women and children in common would be an enormous benefit, if it were possible. The possibility is the other matter, and that's where the real argument will be.'
'I think there's plenty of room for doubt on both counts.'

'You mean we have to fight on two fronts at once,' I said. 'I was hoping to slip away from one of them, by getting you to grant the usefulness, so that only the question of possibility would be left.'
'Well, your little maneuver's been spotted,' he said. 'So you'll have to defend both.'

'All right, I accept my sentence,' I said. 'But do me one small favor. Let me feed my mind on the dream a while, the way people daydream as they walk along alone. Before they've worked out any means of getting what they want, which is a question that never troubles them, they'd rather not tire themselves wondering whether it's possible. They simply assume they already have what they're after and go straight on planning, delighting in spelling out everything they'll do once the wish has come true, the way idle minds go slack instead of doing any real good. I'm starting to go soft myself, so with your permission I'd like to put off the question of possibility for now. I'll assume the thing can be done and go straight to how the rulers would carry it out, and I'll show that nothing would do more good for the state and its guardians. I'll work through the benefits first, with your help, if you don't mind, and come back to the question of possibility afterward.'
'I don't mind. Go ahead.'

'Well then. If our rulers, and their helpers under them, are to deserve the names they carry, the one must be willing to obey and the other able to command. The rulers themselves must obey the laws, and in whatever details are left to their own judgment they must act in the laws' spirit.'
'That's right.'

'You, then, as their lawgiver,' I said, 'having picked out the men, will pick out the women in the same way and assign them to the men, matching them as far as possible in nature. And since they share common houses and common meals, with no one owning anything privately, they'll live together, mingle together in the gymnasium and the rest of their daily life, and so be drawn together by an inner necessity to mate with one another. Or doesn't "necessity" seem to you the right word?'
'Necessity,' he said, 'not the geometer's kind, but the kind lovers know, which is far better at persuading and compelling most people.'
'Quite so,' I said. 'But Glaucon, all this, like everything else, has to go in an orderly way. In a city of the blessed, promiscuity would be an unholy thing, and the rulers won't allow it.'
'No,' he said, 'it shouldn't be allowed.'
'Then clearly the next step is to make marriage as sacred as we can, and the most beneficial marriages will be the ones counted most sacred.'
'Exactly.'

'And how do we make marriages most beneficial? Tell me this, Glaucon, I ask because I see hunting dogs in your house, and quite a few fine birds. Have you ever paid attention to how they pair and breed?'
'In what way?' he asked.
'Well, first of all, even though they're all of good stock, aren't some of them better than the rest?'
'They are.'
'And do you breed from all of them alike, or are you careful to breed only from the best?'
'Only from the best.'
'And do you breed from the youngest, or the oldest, or those in their prime?'
'Those in their prime.'
'And if you didn't breed carefully, you'd expect your dogs and birds to deteriorate badly?'
'Certainly.'
'And it's the same with horses, and animals in general?'
'Of course.'
'Good heavens, my friend,' I said. 'If the same holds for human beings, what consummate skill our rulers are going to need.'
'It does hold,' he said. 'But why does it call for any special skill?'

'Because,' I said, 'our rulers will have to dose the body of the city with a good deal of medicine. You know that when patients don't need drugs but only need to follow a regimen, we think even a second-rate doctor will do. But when drugs have to be given, we know it takes a bolder physician.'
'True, but what are you driving at?'

'I mean,' I said, 'that our rulers will probably have to use a fair dose of falsehood and deception for the good of those they rule. We did say, didn't we, that such things, used as medicine, could be useful.'
'And we were right.'
'Well, it looks as if this lawful use of them will be needed often, in arranging marriages and births.'
'How so?'

'It follows from what we've agreed,' I said, 'that the best men should mate with the best women as often as possible, and the inferior with the inferior as seldom as possible; and that the children of the first sort should be raised, but not the children of the second, if the flock is to stay first-rate. And all this has to happen without anyone knowing but the rulers themselves, if our herd of guardians is to be kept as free as possible of strife.'
'Very true.'

'So we'll need to establish certain festivals at which we bring the brides and grooms together, with sacrifices, and wedding songs composed by our poets to fit the occasion. The number of marriages we'll leave to the rulers, so they can keep the population as steady as possible, taking into account losses from war and disease and the like, and keep the city, as far as they can, from growing too large or too small.'
'Right.'
'And we'll have to devise some clever system of lots, so that on each occasion the less worthy man, when he ends up unmatched, blames his bad luck and not the rulers.'
'Of course.'

'And I should think that among the other honors and prizes we give our braver and better young men, we'll grant them more frequent permission to lie with the women. It will look like a reward for their courage, and at the same time it gives us an excuse for fathering as many children as possible on such men.'
'Right.'
'And the newborns are taken over by officials appointed for the purpose, whether men or women or both, since of course our offices are open to women as well as men.'
'Yes.'

'These officials will take the children of the good parents to a sort of nursery, to nurses living apart in a separate quarter of the city. But the children of the inferior parents, and any born defective to the others, they'll quietly put away, out of sight, as is proper.'
'Yes,' he said, 'if the breed of the guardians is to be kept pure.'

'And these officials will see to the children's feeding, bringing the mothers to the nursery when their breasts are full, but taking every precaution that no mother recognizes her own child. They'll bring in other wet nurses if more are needed. They'll see that the mothers don't nurse too long, and hand over the night feedings and the rest of the trouble to nurses and attendants.'
'You're making childbearing an easy life for the guardians' women.'
'And so it should be,' I said. 'But let's get on with the plan. We said the parents should be in the prime of life.'
'We did.'
'And do you agree that the prime of life is about twenty years for a woman and thirty for a man?'
'Which years do you mean?'

'A woman,' I said, 'should bear children for the state from the age of twenty to the age of forty; a man should beget them from the time he's past his sharpest speed, around twenty-five, until he's fifty-five.'
'Yes,' he said, 'those are the years of physical and mental prime in both.'

'So if a man older or younger than this takes part in fathering children for the community, we'll call it an offense against religion and against right. The child he's gotten, if it slips into life, will have been conceived without the sacrifices and prayers that priestesses and priests and the whole city offer at every marriage festival, praying that the new generation may be better and more useful than their good and useful parents. His child, instead, will be the offspring of darkness and lawless lust.'
'Very true.'

'The same law applies if a man still within the proper age touches one of the women in her prime without a ruler's sanction. We'll say he's foisting a bastard on the state, unauthorized and unconsecrated.'
'Very true.'

'But this holds only while they're within the prescribed ages. After that, we'll let men and women associate freely with whomever they like, except that a man may not touch his daughter or his daughter's daughter, his mother or his mother's mother, and a woman may not touch her son or his son, her father or his father, and so on in either direction. And we grant this freedom only on the strict condition that they do everything they can to see that no child comes of these unions; or if one forces its way to birth, they must understand that no provision will be made for raising it, and act accordingly.'
'That too is reasonable,' he said. 'But how are they to tell who's father and daughter, and the rest, if no one knows?'

'They won't,' I said. 'But it'll work like this. Counting from the day of any marriage festival, a man will call all the children born in the seventh and tenth month after it his sons and daughters, and they'll call him father; he'll call their children his grandchildren, and they'll call him and his generation grandfathers and grandmothers; and all the children conceived in the same season, when their fathers and mothers were paired, will count as brothers and sisters, and these, as I said, won't intermarry. The law won't forbid brothers and sisters absolutely, though: if the lot falls their way and the oracle at Delphi consents, it will allow it.'
'Quite right,' he said.

'So that, Glaucon, is how the guardians of our state are to hold their women and children in common. Now we need the argument to confirm that this arrangement fits the rest of our constitution, and that nothing could be better. Isn't that the next thing?'
'Yes, certainly.'

'Then let's start by asking ourselves this: what should a lawmaker aim at, above all, in framing laws and ordering a state? What's the greatest good, and what's the greatest evil? Then we can ask whether what we've described bears the stamp of the good or of the evil.'
'By all means.'
'Is there any greater evil for a state than what splits it apart and makes it many instead of one? Or any greater good than what binds it together and makes it one?'
'There isn't.'
'And isn't a state bound into one when its citizens share their pleasures and pains, all glad together and all grieved together over the same gains and losses?'
'No doubt of it.'
'Whereas it's torn apart when feeling isn't shared but private, when the same events in the city or among the citizens leave one set of people overjoyed and another plunged in grief?'
'Certainly.'
'And doesn't that kind of split come from people not saying "mine" and "not mine" about the same things, and the same with "his" and "not his"?'
'Exactly.'
'So the best-ordered state is the one where the largest number of people apply the words "mine" and "not mine" in the same way to the same thing?'
'Quite true.'

'The state, in other words, that comes closest to a single person. When one of us hurts a finger, the whole partnership of body and soul, organized as one thing under the ruling part within it, feels the hurt and suffers along with the part that's hurt, and we say the man has a pain in his finger. It's the same with any other part of him, whether it suffers pain or finds relief.'
'It is,' he said. 'And I agree, the best-ordered state comes nearest to this shared feeling you describe.'
'So when anything good or bad happens to one of its citizens, a state like this will take his case as its own, and the whole city will rejoice or grieve with him?'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's what happens in a well-run state.'
'Then it's time,' I said, 'to go back to our own state and see whether it, or some other arrangement, best matches these principles.'
'Very good.'
'Our state, like every other, has rulers and ruled?'
'It does.'
'All of whom call one another citizens?'
'Of course.'
'But in other states, what do the people call their rulers, besides citizens?'
'In most they call them masters; in democracies they just call them rulers.'
'And in our state, what name do the people give the rulers besides citizens?'
'Saviors and protectors,' he said.
'And what do the rulers call the people?'
'Their providers and supporters.'
'And in other states, what do rulers call the people?'
'Slaves.'
'And what do rulers in other states call one another?'
'Fellow rulers.'
'And in ours?'
'Fellow guardians.'
'Now, in other states, can a ruler speak of one of his colleagues as a friend and another as no friend of his?'
'Yes, often enough.'
'And he thinks and speaks of the friend as one of his own, and the other as an outsider, no concern of his?'
'Exactly.'
'But would any of your guardians ever think or speak of a fellow guardian as an outsider?'
'Never,' he said. 'Everyone he meets he'll regard as a brother or sister, a father or mother, a son or daughter, or the child or parent of one of these.'

'Well put,' I said. 'But tell me one more thing. Will they be family in name only, or will they back the name up in everything they do? Take the word "father." Will it carry with it a father's care, and the reverence and obedience the law commands toward a parent, so that a man who fails in these is seen as godless and unjust, the kind no one expects much good of from gods or men? Are these to be the refrains the children hear from everyone, from the moment they're told who their parents and kin are, or not?'
'These and no others,' he said. 'For what could be more ridiculous than mouthing the names of family ties without living up to them?'
'So in our city, more than in any other, when things go well or badly with one of them, all will say with one voice, "It goes well with me" or "It goes badly with me."'
'Very true.'
'And we said this way of speaking and thinking goes hand in hand with sharing their pleasures and pains?'
'Yes, and so they will.'
'They'll share a common interest in the same thing, which they'll all call their own, and sharing it, they'll share the same pleasure and pain?'
'Far more than in other states.'
'And the cause of this, on top of the rest of the constitution, is the guardians' holding women and children in common?'
'That, above all.'
'And we agreed this unity of feeling is the greatest good for a state, comparing a well-ordered state to a body sharing in the pleasure and pain of its parts?'
'We did, and rightly.'
'Then the community of women and children among our guardians is clearly the source of the greatest good to the state?'
'Certainly.'

'And this fits what we said before, that the guardians were to have no houses or land or any other property; their pay was to be their keep, provided by the other citizens, and they'd have no private expenses, so that they could stay true guardians.'
'Right.'

'So both arrangements, the shared property and the shared family, make them more truly guardians. They won't tear the city apart by disagreeing over what's "mine" and "not mine," each man hauling whatever he's gotten off into his own private house, with his own private wife and children and his own private pleasures and pains. No, they'll all be moved as far as possible by the same pleasures and pains, because they're all of one mind about what's near and dear to them, and so they all pull toward a single goal.'
'Just so.'

'And since they have nothing they can call their own but their bodies, there'll be no lawsuits and no accusations among them. They'll be free of all the quarrels people fall into over money, children, and relatives.'
'They'll have to be.'

'Nor will there be any prosecutions for assault or insult among them. We'll say it's a fine and proper thing for a man to defend himself against an equal, and that protecting one's own body is a duty.'
'That's good,' he said.
'And there's a further benefit in this law: if a man does get angry with another, he'll vent his anger then and there, and it won't grow into something more dangerous.'
'Certainly.'
'The older man will be given authority to rule and discipline the younger.'
'Clearly.'

'And it's plain the younger man won't strike an elder or do him any other violence, unless the rulers order it, and won't show him disrespect either. Two guardians will hold him back, shame and fear: shame, which keeps a man from laying hands on those who stand to him as parents; and fear that the injured man's many defenders, his brothers and sons and fathers, will rush to his aid.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's how it would go.'
'So in every way the laws will help these men keep peace with one another?'
'Yes, there'll be plenty of peace.'
'And since the guardians won't quarrel among themselves, there's no danger the rest of the city will break into factions, either against them or against each other.'
'None at all.'

'There are smaller miseries they'll be rid of too, though I'm almost ashamed to mention them, they're so petty: the flattery of the rich by the poor, the whole grind of raising a household and scraping together money, the borrowing and then denying the debt, the getting of cash by any means and handing it over to wife and slaves to manage. All the many indignities people put up with in this line are obvious and beneath mention.'
'Obvious indeed,' he said. 'A man doesn't need eyes to see them.'
'They'll be freed from all of it, and their life will be blessed, more blessed even than the life of victors at the Olympic games.'
'How so?'

'The Olympic victor,' I said, 'is counted happy for winning only a fraction of what's secured to our citizens. Their victory is the finer one, and their keep at the public expense more complete. For the prize they've won is nothing less than the salvation of the whole state, and the crown set on them and their children is everything life needs. They're honored by their country while they live, and given an honorable burial when they die.'
'Yes,' he said, 'those are glorious rewards.'

'Do you remember,' I said, 'how earlier on someone, who shall stay nameless, accused us of making our guardians miserable, men who could have owned everything and instead owned nothing? And we answered that we'd take that up another time if the chance came, but for now we were making our guardians true guardians, and shaping the state with a view to the greatest happiness not of any one class but of the whole?'
'Yes, I remember.'

'Well, now that the life of our protectors turns out to be far better and nobler than an Olympic victor's, is there any comparing it with the life of a shoemaker, or any other craftsman, or a farmer?'
'Certainly not.'

'Still, I'll repeat here what I said before: if any of our guardians tries to be happy in a way that stops him being a guardian, if he isn't content with this safe and harmonious life, which we judge to be the best of all, but gets some foolish, youthful notion of happiness into his head and tries to seize the whole state for himself, he'll learn how wise Hesiod was when he said that, somehow, the half is more than the whole.'
'If he asked my advice,' he said, 'I'd tell him to stay where he is, with a life like that on offer.'

'You agree, then,' I said, 'that the men and women are to share their whole way of life, as we've described, sharing their education, sharing their children, and sharing the work of guarding the citizens, whether at home or out at war, keeping watch and hunting together like dogs, and in all things, as far as they're able, the women sharing with the men? And in doing this they'll do what's best, and won't violate the natural relation of the sexes but preserve it.'
'I agree.'
'Then what's left to ask,' I said, 'is whether such a community is even possible among human beings, as it is among other animals, and if so, how.'
'You've taken the words out of my mouth,' he said.
'As for the war part,' I said, 'there's no difficulty seeing how they'll manage that.'
'How do you mean?'

'They'll go on campaign together, of course, and take along any of their children who are old enough, so the young ones can watch the work they'll have to do as adults, the way an artisan's child watches the trade. And besides watching, they'll help out and make themselves useful in war, and wait on their fathers and mothers. Haven't you noticed in the crafts how a potter's boys watch and assist for a long time before they ever touch the wheel?'
'I have.'
'And should potters take more care than our guardians to school their children by letting them watch and practice their work?'
'That would be absurd.'
'Besides, every creature fights harder in the presence of its young, and the same goes for our guardians.'
'True, Socrates. But there's a real danger here, the kind that often comes in war: if they're defeated, they lose the children along with themselves, and the state can never recover.'
'True,' I said. 'But would you have them run no risk at all, ever?'
'Far from it.'
'Well, then, if they're ever to face danger, shouldn't it be the kind that, if they come through it, leaves them the better for it?'
'Clearly.'
'And isn't it important enough, whether men who are to be soldiers see war in their youth or not, to be worth running some risk for?'
'Yes, very important.'
'So our first step is to make our children spectators of war. But we must also see to it they're kept safe, and then all will be well.'
'Right.'
'Now their parents, presumably, won't be blind to the dangers of war, but will know as well as human foresight allows which campaigns are safe and which dangerous?'
'We can assume that.'
'So they'll bring the children along on the safe ones and steer clear of the dangerous?'
'Yes.'
'And they'll put them under the command of seasoned veterans, fit to be their leaders and teachers?'
'As they should.'
'Still, the dangers of war can't always be foreseen; there's a lot of chance in it.'
'True.'
'Then against just such chances, the children should be fitted with wings from the start, so they can fly off and escape if the need arises.'
'What do you mean?' he asked.

'I mean we should put them on horseback in their earliest years, and once they've learned to ride, take them mounted to see the fighting. The horses mustn't be spirited war-horses, but the gentlest we can find that are still fast. That way the children get a good look at what will one day be their own work, and if danger comes they only have to follow their elder leaders and ride to safety.'
'I think you're right,' he said.

'Now as for war itself, how should your soldiers behave toward one another and toward the enemy? I'd suggest that any soldier who deserts his post, or throws away his weapons, or shows any other cowardice, should be demoted to the rank of farmer or craftsman. What do you say?'
'By all means.'
'And the man who lets himself be taken alive, we may as well make a gift of him to his captors; he's their lawful prize, to do with as they please.'
'Certainly.'
'But the hero who has distinguished himself, what's to be done with him? First, while still on campaign, he should be crowned in turn by each of the young men who served beside him. What do you say?'
'I approve.'
'And what about each of them clasping his hand?'
'That too.'
'But you'll hardly approve my next proposal.'
'What is it?'
'That he should kiss and be kissed by each of them.'

'Most of all,' he said. 'And I'd add to the law that, for as long as the campaign lasts, no one he's minded to kiss may refuse him, so that if a man is in love with someone in the army, man or woman, he'll be all the keener to win the prize of valor.'

'Excellent,' I said. 'And we've already settled that the brave man is to have more marriages than the rest, and to be chosen for them more often than others, so that as many children as possible may be fathered on such a man.'
'We have.'

'And there's another way, on Homer's authority, that brave young men should be honored. Homer tells how Ajax, after distinguishing himself in battle, was rewarded with the long cut of the chine, a fitting tribute, it seems, to a hero in his prime, since it's both an honor and a thing to build his strength.'
'Quite right.'

'Then in this,' I said, 'we'll take Homer as our teacher. At sacrifices and the like, we'll honor the brave according to their courage, men and women alike, with hymns and the other distinctions we mentioned, and also with',
'"seats of honor, and meat, and brimming cups,"',
'and in honoring them this way, we'll be training them at the same time.'
'Excellent,' he said.
'And when a man dies gloriously in war, won't we say first of all that he belongs to the golden race?'
'Surely.'
'And don't we have Hesiod's word for it that when men of that race die,',
'"they become holy spirits upon the earth, doers of good, wardens against evil, guardians of mortal men"?'
'Yes, and we accept his word.'
'Then we'll ask the god how we're to bury these godlike, heroic men, and what special honors to give them, and we'll do as he directs.'
'By all means.'

'And forever after we'll revere their graves and kneel at their tombs as at the tombs of spirits. And the same honors will go to any others judged outstandingly good, who die of old age or in any other way.'
'That's quite right,' he said.
'Next, how should our soldiers treat their enemies?'
'In what respect?'

'Take slavery first. Do you think it right for Greeks to enslave Greek cities, or to stand by while others do it, if they can prevent it? Shouldn't their rule be to spare them, mindful of the danger that the whole Greek race might one day fall under the yoke of foreigners?'
'Sparing them is infinitely better.'
'So they'll hold no Greek as a slave, and advise the other Greeks to do the same.'
'Certainly,' he said. 'That way they'll stand together against the foreigner and keep their hands off one another.'

'And the slain, should the victors strip them of anything but their armor? Doesn't the habit of plundering the dead give cowards an excuse not to face the living? Many an army has been lost before now to this love of loot, with men skulking over corpses, pretending they're doing their duty.'
'Very true.'

'And isn't there something low and greedy in robbing a corpse, something mean and womanish in treating the dead body as the enemy when the real enemy has flown off and left only his fighting gear behind? It's like a dog that can't reach the man who threw the stone, and snaps at the stone instead.'
'Very like a dog,' he said.
'So we'll have nothing to do with stripping the dead, or refusing to let them be buried?'
'Nothing whatever,' he said.

'Nor will we hang up captured arms in the temples as offerings, least of all the arms of Greeks, if we mean to keep on good terms with the other Greeks. In fact we have reason to fear that offering up spoils taken from our kinsmen would be a kind of pollution, unless the god himself commands it.'
'Very true.'
'And what about ravaging Greek land or burning Greek houses? How should our soldiers behave?'
'I'd be glad to hear your view,' he said.
'My judgment is that both should be forbidden, and that they should carry off only the year's harvest. Shall I tell you why?'
'Please.'

'It's this. There are two different words, "discord" and "war," and I think they answer to two different things. One names what's internal and at home among kin, the other what's foreign and against outsiders. The strife among one's own we call discord; only the strife with outsiders do we call war.'
'That's a sound distinction.'
'And isn't it just as sound to say that the whole Greek race is bound together by blood and kinship, and is foreign and alien to the non-Greek world?'
'Quite right.'

'So when Greeks fight non-Greeks, and non-Greeks Greeks, we'll say they're at war, being enemies by nature, and this kind of conflict should be called war. But when Greeks fight Greeks, we'll say Greece is sick and torn by discord, since they're friends by nature. That kind of enmity should be called discord.'
'I agree.'

'Then consider,' I said, 'what happens in a case of what we're calling discord, when a city is divided against itself: if each side lays waste the other's land and burns its houses, how monstrous the feud appears. No true patriot could bring himself to tear at his own nurse and mother. It's bearable for the winners to take the losers' harvest, so long as they remember they mean one day to be reconciled, and don't intend to go on fighting forever.'
'Yes,' he said, 'that's a far better spirit than the other.'
'Now the city you're founding will be a Greek city, won't it?'
'It will have to be.'
'And its citizens will be good and civilized?'
'Very civilized.'
