'And won't they love their fellow Greeks, and think of Greece as their own land, and share in its common shrines?'
'Most certainly.'
'So any conflict with other Greeks, since they're their own people, they'll treat as discord and not call war?'
'They won't call it war.'
'And they'll quarrel as men who mean some day to be reconciled?'
'Yes.'
'They'll bring their opponents to their senses in a friendly way, not punish them with slavery or destruction; they'll be correctors, not enemies.'
'Just so.'

'And being Greeks themselves, they won't lay waste Greek land or burn Greek houses, and they'll never suppose that a whole city, men, women, and children alike, is their enemy. They know the guilt of any quarrel always falls on a few, and that most of the people are their friends. So they'll be reluctant to ruin the land or raze the houses, and they'll press the conflict only until the guilty few are forced by the many innocent sufferers to make amends.'
'I agree,' he said, 'that our citizens should treat their Greek enemies this way, and treat non-Greeks the way Greeks now treat each other.'
'Then let's lay down this law too for our guardians: they're not to ravage land or burn houses among the Greeks.'
'Agreed,' he said. 'And we may agree, as with all our earlier provisions, that these are good.'

'But I have to say, Socrates, that if you're allowed to go on like this, you'll forget the question you brushed aside at the start of all this: whether such a state is even possible, and if so, how. I'm quite ready to grant that your plan, if it could be realized, would do the state every kind of good. I'll even add what you left out: your citizens will be the bravest of soldiers, since they all know one another and call each other father, brother, son; and if the women march with them, whether in the same line or behind it, to terrify the enemy or to reinforce them in a pinch, I'm sure they'll be utterly unbeatable. And there are many advantages at home you haven't mentioned, which I freely grant as well. But since I'm granting all of these, and as many more as you like, on the one condition that the state actually exists, let's say no more about them. Let's just assume it exists, and now turn to the one thing left: whether it's possible, and how.'

'You spring on me the moment I pause,' I said, 'and give me no quarter. I've barely escaped the first and second waves, and now, without seeming to notice, you're bringing down on me the third, the biggest and most crushing of all. When you've seen and heard it, you'll understand my hesitation, and forgive me for being slow to take up a proposal so strange as the one I now have to state and examine.'
'The more you talk like that,' he said, 'the less we'll let you off telling us how such a state is possible. So out with it, and quickly.'
'Let me begin by reminding you,' I said, 'that we came to all this in the course of searching for justice and injustice.'
'True. But what of it?'

'Only this. Suppose we've found what justice is. Are we then to demand that the just man fall short of perfect justice in nothing, or will we be content if he comes close, and has more justice in him than other men?'
'Coming close will be enough.'

'We were looking for justice itself, then, and for what the perfectly just man would be like, and for injustice and the perfectly unjust man, so that we'd have a pattern to measure ourselves against. We meant to look at these in order to judge our own happiness or unhappiness by how far we resembled them, not to prove that such people could actually exist.'
'True.'
'Would a painter be any worse a painter if he drew a perfectly beautiful man with consummate skill, but couldn't prove such a man could ever exist?'
'Not in the least.'
'Well, weren't we doing the same, drawing in words a pattern of a good state?'
'We were.'
'Then is our account any worse because we can't prove that a state ordered as we've described could actually come to be?'
'Of course not.'

'That's the truth of it,' I said. 'But if, to please you, I'm to try to show how, and on what conditions, it could come closest to being possible, then I have to ask you to grant me, with that aim in view, the same admissions as before.'
'Which admissions?'

'This one: can anything ever be realized in practice exactly as it's described in words? Doesn't the word always reach beyond the fact, so that the actual thing, whatever anyone thinks, must in the nature of things fall a little short of the truth? What do you say?'
'I agree.'

'Then don't insist that I prove the actual state will match the pattern in every detail. If we can show how a city might be governed in the way nearest to what we've described, you'll admit we've found the possibility you demanded, and be satisfied. I would be. Wouldn't you?'
'Yes, I would.'

'Then let me try to point out what flaw it is in states that keeps them from being governed this way, and what smallest change would let a state cross over into the better form, one change if possible, or if not, two, but in any case as few and as slight as can be.'
'By all means.'
'I think,' I said, 'that the state could be transformed by a single change, though not a slight or easy one, still a possible one.'
'What is it?' he asked.
'Here, then,' I said, 'I come to the thing I likened to the greatest wave. Yet it shall be spoken, even if the wave breaks over me in a flood of laughter and contempt and drowns me. Listen closely.'
'Go on.'

'Unless philosophers become kings in their cities, or those we now call kings and rulers take genuinely and adequately to philosophy, so that political power and wisdom meet in the same person, while the many natures who now pursue one apart from the other are forcibly barred from doing so, there will be no rest from evils, Glaucon, for cities, nor I think for the human race; and our city, the one we've been describing in words, will never come into being and see the light of day. This is what I shrank from saying so long, seeing how very strange it would sound; for it's hard to face the fact that there's no other road to happiness, public or private.'

'Socrates,' he said, 'after a statement like that, you'd better expect a great many people, and not unimpressive ones, to come at you. Picture them throwing off their coats on the spot, stripped for action, snatching up whatever weapon's nearest, and rushing at you full tilt, ready to do who knows what. If you don't have an argument ready to hold them off, you'll be cut to pieces by their scorn, and serve you right.'
'And it was you,' I said, 'who got me into this scrape.'

'And I was right to,' he said. 'But I won't abandon you. I'll do what I can, which is to offer goodwill and encouragement, and maybe answer your questions a bit more obligingly than someone else would. With an ally like that, do your best to show the doubters you're right.'

'I'll have to try,' I said, 'since you offer such priceless help. And I think the first thing we need, if we're to have any hope of escape, is to explain to them exactly whom we mean when we dare to say that philosophers should rule. Once that's clear, we can defend ourselves by showing that some natures are born for philosophy and for leading the state, while others aren't, and are meant to follow rather than lead.'
'Then it's time for a definition,' he said.
'Follow me,' I said, 'and let's see if somehow we can lay it out properly.'
'Lead on.'

'I'll have to remind you of something, or rather, you'll remember it without my help: if we call a man a lover of something, and the name fits, he must love not one part of that thing but the whole of it.'
'I'm afraid I don't follow. You'll have to jog my memory.'

'That answer would suit someone else, Glaucon,' I said, 'but a man with your eye for these things should know that everyone in the bloom of youth somehow stirs and stings a lover's heart, and strikes him as worthy of his attention. Isn't that how you all treat your favorites? One has a snub nose, and you call it charming; another's is hooked, and you say it has a royal look; the one in between, you praise for perfect proportion. The dark are manly, the fair are children of the gods, and even "honey-pale," what is that but a lover's pet name for sallow skin, forgiven so long as it's on the cheek of youth? In a word, you'll seize on any excuse and say anything rather than let a single flower of that springtime go by.'
'If you want to make me your example of how lovers behave,' he said, 'I'll go along with it, for the argument's sake.'
'And lovers of wine,' I said, 'don't you see them doing the same? Any excuse will do to drink any wine.'
'Of course.'

'And it's the same with ambitious men. If they can't command an army, they'll command a company; if they can't be honored by the great and important, they're glad to be honored by lesser, meaner people. Honor of some kind they must have.'
'Exactly.'
'Then tell me this. When a man desires something, do we say he desires the whole of that kind of thing, or only a part?'
'The whole.'
'Then shall we say of the philosopher too that he loves not part of wisdom but the whole of it?'
'The whole.'

'And the man who turns up his nose at learning, especially while he's young and can't yet judge what's worth knowing, we'll deny is a philosopher or a lover of learning, just as we'd say a man who has no appetite for his food isn't hungry, but has a poor appetite rather than a good one?'
'Quite right.'
'Whereas the man who's eager for every kind of learning, curious and never satisfied, him we may fairly call a philosopher, a lover of wisdom. Don't you agree?'

'If that's all it takes,' said Glaucon, 'curiosity, then you'll find a great many odd characters claiming the title. All the lovers of spectacles delight in learning, after a fashion, so they'd have to count. And the music lovers are a strange lot to file under philosophers, the very last people you could drag to anything like a serious discussion, yet they run from one Dionysian festival to the next as though they'd hired out their ears to hear every chorus, and miss none, in town or country. Are we really going to call all these people philosophers, along with the dabblers in every trifling art?'
'Certainly not,' I said. 'They're only an imitation of the real thing.'
'Then who are the true philosophers?' he asked.
'Those,' I said, 'who love the sight of truth.'
'That's well said too,' he replied. 'But what do you mean by it?'
'It wouldn't be easy to explain to just anyone,' I said. 'But you, I'm sure, will grant me something I'm about to propose.'
'What's that?'
'That since beauty and ugliness are opposites, they're two things?'
'Of course.'
'And since they're two, each of them is one?'
'That too.'

'And the same holds for just and unjust, good and bad, and every other such kind: each, taken by itself, is one. But because they show up everywhere, mixed in with actions and bodies and one another, each of them appears as many.'
'That's true.'

'And this is the line I draw between the two groups: on one side those lovers of spectacle and craft and practical affairs you spoke of, and on the other those I'm calling the only ones who really deserve the name of philosopher.'
'How do you mean?' he asked.

'The lovers of sounds and sights,' I said, 'are devoted to beautiful tones and colors and shapes, and everything fashioned out of them, but their minds are unable to see beauty itself, or to love it.'
'True.'
'And those able to reach beauty itself, and to see it as it is in itself, aren't they rare?'
'Very rare.'

'So a man who recognizes beautiful things but not beauty itself, and who can't follow if someone tries to lead him to the knowledge of it, do you think he's living awake, or only dreaming? Think about it: isn't a dreamer, asleep or awake, exactly the man who takes the likeness of a thing for the thing itself?'
'I'd certainly say such a man is dreaming.'

'But the other, who recognizes that there is a beauty itself and can see both it and the things that share in it, without mistaking the things for it or it for the things, is he awake, or dreaming too?'
'Wide awake.'
'So we'd be right to say his state of mind is knowledge, since he knows, and the other man's is opinion, since he only forms opinions?'
'Certainly.'

'But suppose this second man, the one we say only has opinions and not knowledge, takes offense and disputes what we're saying. Can we find some way to soothe him and win him over gently, without letting on that he isn't quite well in the head?'
'We ought to try.'

'Come, then, let's think of what to say to him. Or rather, let's question him, assuring him that if he knows anything we hold no grudge against him, in fact we'd be glad to find he knows something. But we'll ask him: this man who knows, does he know something, or nothing? Answer for him, Glaucon.'
'I'll answer that he knows something.'
'Something that is, or something that is not?'
'Something that is. How could anything that is not ever be known?'
'So we're satisfied, however many ways we look at it, that what fully is can be fully known, and what in no way is must be wholly unknown?'
'Nothing could be more certain.'
'Good. Now if there's something that both is and is not, won't it lie somewhere between what purely is and what utterly is not?'
'It will.'

'And since knowledge was set over what is, and ignorance, necessarily, over what is not, then for this in-between thing we'll have to find something in between ignorance and knowledge, if there is any such thing?'
'We will.'
'Now do we admit there's such a thing as opinion?'
'Of course.'
'A different power from knowledge, or the same?'
'A different one.'
'So opinion is set over one thing, and knowledge over another, each according to its own power?'
'Yes.'
'And knowledge is set over what is, to know that what is, is. But first I'd better draw a distinction.'
'What distinction?'

'I'll set down powers as a class of their own. They're what enables us, and everything else, to do whatever we can do. Sight and hearing, for instance, I'd call powers, if that makes the class I mean clear to you.'
'Yes, I understand.'

'Then hear how I think of them. In a power I can't see any color or shape or anything of the sort, the kind of feature that lets me tell many things apart. With a power I look only to what it's set over and what it accomplishes, and on that basis I call one power the same as another, and another power different. What has the same field and the same result I call the same power; what has a different field and a different result I call different. Is that how you'd put it too?'
'It is.'
'Then, my friend, answer me this. Do you count knowledge as a power, or in what class do you put it?'
'A power,' he said, 'and the mightiest of them all.'
'And opinion, is that a power too, or some other kind of thing?'
'A power as well,' he said. 'It's just that by which we're able to form opinions.'
'But a moment ago you agreed that knowledge and opinion aren't the same.'
'How could anyone in his right mind treat the infallible as the same as the fallible?'
'Well said,' I replied. 'So we plainly agree that opinion is one thing and knowledge another.'
'We do.'
'So each of them, having a different power, is set over a different thing?'
'It must be.'
'Knowledge is set over what is, to know what is, as it is?'
'Yes.'
'And opinion, we say, forms opinions?'
'Yes.'
'About the same thing knowledge knows? Can the field of opinion and the field of knowledge be one and the same?'

'No,' he replied, 'that's been ruled out already. If different powers are set over different fields, and opinion and knowledge are different powers, as we've agreed, then the field of knowledge and the field of opinion can't be the same.'
'So if what is, is the field of knowledge, the field of opinion must be something other than what is?'
'Yes, something else.'

'Is it, then, what is not? Or rather, can there even be an opinion about what is not? Think: when a man holds an opinion, isn't his opinion about something? Can anyone have an opinion, yet have it about nothing?'
'Impossible.'
'So the man who holds an opinion holds it about some one thing?'
'Yes.'
'But what is not couldn't rightly be called some one thing; it's nothing at all.'
'True.'
'And we were forced to assign ignorance to what is not, and knowledge to what is?'
'Rightly so,' he said.
'Then opinion is set over neither what is nor what is not?'
'Over neither.'
'So opinion is neither ignorance nor knowledge?'
'It seems not.'
'Then does it lie outside both, surpassing knowledge in clarity, or falling below ignorance in darkness?'
'Neither.'
'Then opinion seems to you darker than knowledge, but brighter than ignorance?'
'Much, in both directions.'
'And to lie inside the two, between them?'
'Yes.'
'So opinion would be the in-between thing?'
'No question.'

'Now didn't we say earlier that if something turned up that both is and is not at once, it would lie in between what purely is and what utterly is not, and that the power set over it would be neither knowledge nor ignorance but whatever turned up in between the two?'
'We did.'
'And now, in that in-between space, what has turned up is what we call opinion?'
'It has.'

'So what's left to find is the thing that shares in both, in being and in not-being, and can't rightly be called purely one or the other. If we find it, we can fairly call it the object of opinion, assigning the extremes to the extreme powers and the in-between to the in-between power.'
'Right.'

'With that settled, I'd like to put a question to our friend, the good fellow who denies there's any beauty itself, any unchanging form of the beautiful, and holds instead that the beautiful is a many, the lover of spectacles who can't endure being told that the beautiful is one, or the just is one, or that anything at all is one. I'd say to him: my good man, of all these many beautiful things, is there one that won't also turn up ugly? Of all the just things, one that won't turn up unjust? Of all the holy, one that won't turn up unholy?'
'No,' he said. 'Each of them is bound to look both beautiful and ugly, somehow, and the same with the rest.'
'And the many doubles, aren't they just as much halves? Doubles of one thing, halves of another?'
'Just so.'
'And things we call great or small, heavy or light, won't they answer just as well to the opposite names?'
'Yes, each of them always belongs to both.'
'So with each of these many things, is it any more what we call it than not what we call it?'

'They're like those punning riddles people trade at dinner parties,' he said, 'or the children's riddle about the eunuch and the bat, what he threw and what it was sitting on. These things are riddles in the same way, with a double face. You can't fix any of them firmly in your mind as being, or as not being, or as both, or as neither.'
'Then what will you do with them?' I said. 'Where could they sit better than between being and not-being? They're surely no darker than what is not, no more real than what is.'
'Quite true,' he said.
'So we seem to have found that the mass of conventional notions the many hold about beauty and the rest go tumbling about somewhere in between pure being and pure not-being.'
'We have.'
'And we agreed beforehand that anything of that sort should be called an object of opinion, not of knowledge, the wandering, in-between thing caught by the in-between power.'
'We did.'

'So those who feast their eyes on many beautiful things but can't see beauty itself, or follow anyone who'd lead them to it, who see many just things but not justice itself, and so on, of all of them we'll say they have opinion but not knowledge of the things they opine about.'
'That's certain.'
'But those who can see each thing itself, the things that stay always the same, unchanging, we'll say they know, and don't merely have opinions.'
'That can't be denied either.'

'And we'll say the one group loves and embraces the objects of knowledge, the other the objects of opinion. For these last, you'll remember, are the ones we said were in love with beautiful sounds and colors and the like, but couldn't bear the thought that beauty itself is anything at all.'
'Yes, I remember.'
'So we won't be out of line, will we, in calling them lovers of opinion rather than lovers of wisdom? And will they be very angry with us for it?'
'Not if they take my advice,' he said. 'No one should be angry at the truth.'
'And those who love each thing as it truly is, them we must call lovers of wisdom, and not lovers of opinion?'
'Without a doubt.'

sections.label: Book VI
sections.title: The Philosopher, the Good, and the Divided Line

segments.text: And so, Glaucon, after a long and weary stretch of argument, the true philosophers and the false have finally come into view.
'I don't see how the road could have been any shorter,' he said.

'Probably not,' I said. 'And yet I think we'd have gotten a clearer view of both kinds if we could have kept to this one subject, instead of having all these other questions still waiting for us—the ones anyone has to face who wants to see exactly how the life of the just man differs from the life of the unjust.'
'So what comes next?' he asked.

'Surely the question that follows in order,' I said. 'Since only philosophers are able to grasp what is eternal and unchanging, while those who drift about among the many changing things are not philosophers, which of the two should be the rulers of our city?'
'How should we answer that?'
'Whichever group is better able to guard the laws and institutions of our city—let them be our guardians.'
'Fair enough.'
'And surely there's no question,' I said, 'that a guardian set to watch over something should have eyes rather than no eyes?'
'No question at all.'

'Now, men who truly lack any knowledge of what each thing really is—who carry no clear pattern in their souls, and so can't look, the way a painter looks, toward the absolute truth, return to that original again and again, see it with perfect clarity, and from it set in order our laws about what is beautiful and good and just, where they aren't ordered already, and then keep guard and preserve them—aren't men like that simply blind?'
'Pretty much blind, yes,' he said.
'Then shall we make them our guardians, when there are others who match them in experience and fall short of them in no virtue, and who also know the truth of each thing?'
'It would make no sense,' he said, 'to pass over men who have this greatest of all advantages. As long as they don't fall short in some other way, they have to come first.'
'Then suppose we work out how the same men can have both this knowledge and the other excellences too.'
'By all means.'

'As we said when we started, the first thing is to settle what the philosopher's nature really is. Once we've come to an understanding about that, then—if I'm not mistaken—we'll also agree that this combination of qualities is possible, and that the people who have them, and only they, should rule the city.'
'How do you mean?'
'Let's agree that philosophical minds always love the kind of knowledge that reveals to them the eternal—what doesn't shift with coming-to-be and passing-away.'
'Agreed.'

'And let's also agree,' I said, 'that they love all of that true being, that there's no part of it, great or small, more honorable or less, that they're willing to give up—just as we said before about the lover and the man hungry for honor.'
'True.'
'And if they're to be what we've been describing, isn't there another quality they have to have as well?'
'What quality?'
'Truthfulness. They will never willingly let a falsehood into their minds—they hate it—and they love the truth.'
'That's safe to say of them.'
'"Safe to say" isn't the word, my friend,' I replied. '"Must be said" is the word. A man whose nature is in love with something can't help loving everything that belongs to it or is akin to it.'
'Right,' he said.
'And is there anything more akin to wisdom than truth?'
'How could there be?'
'Can the same nature love wisdom and love falsehood at once?'
'Never.'
'So the genuine lover of learning must, from his earliest youth, reach out for all the truth he can?'
'Absolutely.'
'But we know from experience that when a man's desires run strong in one direction, they run weaker in the others, like a stream that's been drawn off into another channel.'
'True.'

'So a man whose desires flow toward knowledge in every form will be absorbed in the pleasures of the soul itself and will hardly notice the pleasures of the body—that is, if he's a real philosopher and not a fake.'
'Quite certainly.'
'A man like that is bound to be temperate, the very opposite of greedy. The motives that drive other men to grab and spend have no place in his character.'
'Very true.'
'Here's another mark of the philosophical nature to consider.'
'What's that?'
'There must be no hidden streak of pettiness in him. Nothing could be more at odds than smallness of mind with a soul that's always reaching out toward the whole of things, both divine and human.'
'Very true,' he said.
'And how could a man with greatness of mind, who looks out on all of time and all of being, think human life is much of anything?'
'He can't.'
'Or count death as something to fear?'
'Not at all.'
'So the cowardly, petty nature can have no share in true philosophy?'
'Certainly not.'
'And again: a man who is well-balanced—not greedy, not mean, not a braggart, not a coward—could such a man ever be unjust or hard to deal with?'
'Impossible.'

'So when you're looking at a soul, you'll quickly see whether it's just and gentle or harsh and unsociable. Even in the young, these are the signs that mark off the philosophical nature from the rest.'
'True.'
'There's one more point to watch for.'
'What's that?'
'Whether he takes pleasure in learning. No one loves what gives him pain and where, after great labor, he makes little headway.'
'Of course not.'
'And if he's forgetful, and holds on to nothing of what he learns, won't he end up an empty vessel?'
'He certainly will.'
'Laboring for nothing, he's bound to end up hating himself and hating the work?'
'Yes.'
'So a forgetful soul can't be counted among the genuine philosophical natures. We have to insist that the philosopher have a good memory.'
'Certainly.'
'And a nature that's clumsy and out of tune can only tend toward things being out of proportion?'
'No doubt.'
'And do you take truth to be akin to proportion, or to the lack of it?'
'To proportion.'
'So along with the rest, we have to look for a mind that's naturally well-proportioned and gracious, one that moves of its own accord toward the true being of each thing.'
'Certainly.'
'Well now—don't all the qualities we've been listing belong together, and aren't they, in a way, all necessary to a soul that's going to share fully and completely in being?'
'They're absolutely necessary,' he replied.

'And isn't this a study without reproach, one that only a man can pursue who has the gift of a good memory, is quick to learn, noble, gracious, and a friend to truth, justice, courage, and temperance—his own kindred?'
'Even the god of envy himself,' he said, 'could find no fault with such a study.'
'And it's to men like this,' I said, 'once they're brought to maturity by years and education, and to these alone, that you'll hand over the city.'

Here Adeimantus broke in. 'Socrates,' he said, 'no one can argue against these statements of yours, point by point. But here's what happens to the people listening when you talk this way: they feel that, because they aren't skilled at asking and answering questions, they're being led just a little off course at each step of the argument, and the littles pile up, until at the end of the discussion they find themselves badly beaten—everything they used to think turned completely upside down. It's like a game of draughts: unskilled players are finally cornered by the better ones until they've no move left to make. So too your listeners are finally cornered, with nothing to say, in this other game where the counters are words instead of pieces—and yet they feel that all along the truth is on their side. I say this because of what's happening right now. Anyone of us might admit that, although in words he can't meet you at each step, he sees as a plain fact that the people who take up philosophy—not just briefly in their youth as part of an education, but as the pursuit of their mature years—most of them turn into very strange creatures, not to say downright scoundrels, and that even the best of them are made useless to the world by the very study you're praising.'
'Well,' I said, 'do you think the people who say this are wrong?'
'I can't tell,' he replied. 'I'd like to hear your opinion.'
'Here's my answer: I think they're quite right.'
'Then how can you be justified in saying that cities will never be free of evil until philosophers rule them, when we ourselves admit that philosophers are useless to those cities?'
'The question you're asking,' I said, 'can only be answered with an image.'
'And of course,' he said, 'that's something you never do.'

'I see you're enjoying yourself, having dragged me into a discussion that looks hopeless. Now hear the image, and you'll be even more amused at how poor my imagination is—because the way the best men are treated by their own cities is so harsh that nothing on earth quite matches it. So if I'm going to plead their case, I'll have to put my picture together out of many things, the way painters make those mongrel creatures, half goat and half stag. Picture, then, a fleet, or a single ship, set up like this. There's a shipowner, taller and stronger than anyone else aboard, but a little deaf, a little short-sighted, and his knowledge of navigation is about on the same level. The sailors are all quarreling with one another over the steering, each one convinced he has the right to take the helm, though he's never learned the art, can't say who taught him or when he studied it, and will even insist that it can't be taught—and is ready to cut to pieces anyone who says otherwise. They crowd around the shipowner, begging and pleading with him to hand over the tiller; and when they don't get their way and someone else is chosen instead, they kill the rivals or throw them overboard. Then they drug the noble owner with wine or some narcotic, or knock him out some other way, take command of the ship, help themselves to the stores, and so go drinking and feasting their way along on a voyage you'd expect from men like that. On top of this, they call "sailor," "navigator," "master of the craft," any man who's clever at helping them seize the ship from the owner, by force or by persuasion, and they sneer at anyone else as useless. As for the real navigator—that he has to pay attention to the year and the seasons, the sky, the stars, the winds, and everything else that belongs to his art, if he's truly going to be fit to command a ship—they have no idea. They don't see how anyone could combine the skill of steering with the actual command, whether the rest like it or not; they've never even made that part of their trade. With all this going on aboard ship, don't you think the crew of such a vessel would write off the true navigator as a useless babbler, a stargazer, a good-for-nothing?'
'Of course they would,' said Adeimantus.
'Then I don't suppose you need me to spell out what the image means—that this is the philosopher's situation in relation to the city. You see it already.'
'Clearly.'
'Then take this image to the man who's surprised that philosophers get no honor in their cities. Explain it to him, and try to convince him that it would be far more surprising if they were honored.'
'I will.'

'Tell him he's right to think the best of the philosophers are useless to the rest of the world—but tell him to blame their uselessness on the people who refuse to use them, not on the philosophers. It isn't natural for the navigator to beg the sailors to be ruled by him. And as for the clever saying that "the wise go to the doors of the rich"—whoever coined it was lying. The truth is the other way around: when a man is sick, rich or poor, it's he who must go to the doctor, and anyone who needs to be governed must go to the man who can govern. It's not for the ruler who's any good to plead with his subjects to be ruled—though the people who govern us now are a different breed, and they really do deserve to be compared to those mutinous sailors, while the true pilots are exactly the ones those sailors call useless stargazers.'
'Just so,' he said.

'And for these reasons, and among men like these, philosophy—the noblest pursuit of all—is unlikely to be held in much honor by those on the opposing side. But the worst and most lasting damage isn't done to her by her enemies. It's done by her own self-proclaimed followers—the very ones your accuser had in mind when he said that the greater number of them are out-and-out rogues, and the best of them useless. And I agreed.'
'You did.'
'And we've now explained why the good ones are useless?'
'True.'
'Then shall we go on to show that the corruption of the majority is also unavoidable, and that this too is no more philosophy's fault than the other was?'
'By all means.'

'Let's take it in turn, asking and answering, going back first to our description of the gentle and noble nature. Truth, you'll remember, was his leader; he followed her always and in everything. Fail in that, and he was a fraud, with no part or share in true philosophy.'
'Yes, that's what we said.'
'And isn't this one point alone, to name no others, badly at odds with the way people picture him now?'
'Certainly,' he said.

'And don't we have every right to say in his defense that the true lover of knowledge is always straining after being—that this is his nature; that he won't linger among the many individual things that are only appearances, but will press on, the keen edge of his desire never blunted, never slackening, until he has grasped the real nature of each thing with the part of his soul that's fit to grasp it, the part akin to it; and that, drawing near to real being and merging with it through that kinship, he begets intelligence and truth, and so comes to know, and to live and grow truly, and only then—not before—is released from the labor of his striving?'
'Nothing could be more just than that description of him,' he said.
'And will any love of falsehood be part of such a man's nature? Won't he hate a lie with all his soul?'
'He will.'
'And when truth is the leader, we can't suspect any evil in the band she leads?'
'Impossible.'
'Justice and soundness of mind will be in that company, and temperance will come along behind?'
'True,' he replied.

'There's no need for me to line up the philosopher's virtues all over again—you'll remember that courage, greatness of mind, quickness to learn, and memory were his natural gifts. And you objected that, while no one could deny what I said then, still, if you set words aside and look at the facts, some of the men so described are plainly useless and most of them thoroughly corrupt. So we set out to look into the grounds for these charges, and we've now reached the question of why the majority are bad—which forced us back, of necessity, to examining and defining the true philosopher.'
'Exactly.'

'And we have to consider next how the philosophic nature gets corrupted—why so many are ruined and so few escape ruin. I mean the ones we called useless but not wicked. After that, we'll talk about the imitators of philosophy, the men who push into a calling that's beyond them and unworthy of them, and who, by all their inconsistencies, bring down on philosophy and on every philosopher the bad name we're talking about.'
'What are these corruptions?' he asked.
'I'll try to explain. Everyone will agree that a nature with all the qualities we required in a philosopher, brought to perfection, is a rare growth, seldom found among men.'
'Rare indeed.'
'And think how many powerful forces work to destroy these rare natures!'
'What forces?'

'In the first place, their own virtues—their courage, their temperance, and the rest. Each one of these praiseworthy qualities (and here's the strangest thing of all) can ruin the soul that has them and drag it away from philosophy.'
'That is very strange,' he replied.

'Then there are all the ordinary good things of life—beauty, wealth, strength, family connections, influence in the city, you know the sort of thing—and these too have a corrupting, distracting effect.'
'I understand. But I'd like you to say more exactly what you mean.'
'Take hold of the truth as a whole, in the right way,' I said, 'and you'll have no trouble with what I just said; it won't seem strange anymore.'
'And how am I to do that?' he asked.

'We know,' I said, 'that any seed or any growing thing, plant or animal, that fails to get the food, climate, and soil that suit it, is—the more vigorous it is—all the more harmed by the lack of what it needs; for what is good is more an enemy to evil than what is merely indifferent.'
'Very true.'
'So it stands to reason that the finest natures, under unsuitable conditions, suffer more harm than ordinary ones, because the gap between them and their surroundings is greater.'
'Certainly.'

'And mustn't we say, Adeimantus, that the most gifted minds, when they're badly educated, turn out exceptionally bad? Don't the great crimes and the spirit of sheer evil spring from a rich nature ruined by its upbringing, rather than from any weakness, while feeble natures are scarcely capable of any great good or any great evil?'
'There I think you're right.'

'And our philosopher follows the same pattern. Given the right nurture, he must grow up into the fullness of every virtue; but if he's sown and planted in the wrong soil, he becomes the most poisonous of all weeds—unless some divine power saves him. Do you really believe, as people so often say, that it's the Sophists who corrupt our young men, or that private teachers of the art do them any real harm worth mentioning? Isn't the public itself the greatest Sophist of all? Doesn't the public train young and old, men and women alike, to perfection, and shape them after its own heart?'
'And when does that happen?' he asked.

'When they crowd together,' I said, 'and the people sit packed in an assembly, or a courtroom, or a theater, or a camp, or wherever the crowd gathers, and with a great uproar they shout their praise of some things being said or done and their blame of others, both overdone, roaring and clapping their hands—and the rocks and the place they're in echo back and double the noise of their praise and their blame. In a scene like that, won't a young man's heart, as they say, leap inside him? What private training could possibly let him stand firm against such an overwhelming flood of popular opinion? Won't he be swept away on the current, taking up the public's notions of good and bad, doing what they do and becoming what they are?'
'He's bound to, Socrates,' he said.
'And yet,' I said, 'there's a still greater compulsion we haven't mentioned.'
'What's that?'
'The gentle persuasion of disenfranchisement, confiscation, and death, which, as you know, these new Sophists and teachers—the public—bring to bear when their words fail.'
'They certainly do, and they mean it.'
'So what teaching, from any other Sophist or any private man, could be expected to win out in such an unequal contest?'
'None,' he replied.

'No indeed,' I said. 'Even to try is great folly. There neither is, nor has been, nor ever will be, a character formed in any virtue other than the one the public's training supplies—I'm speaking of human virtue, my friend; what is more than human, as the proverb says, isn't included. For I'd not have you forget that, in the present wretched state of government, whatever is saved and comes out well is saved by the power of God—and we can say that truly.'
'I quite agree,' he replied.
'Then let me ask you to agree to one more thing.'
'What are you going to say?'

'That all those hired men whom the many call Sophists and treat as their rivals in fact teach nothing but the opinions of the many—the very views the crowds form in their assemblies—and they call this wisdom. It's as if a man kept a great, strong beast and made a study of its moods and appetites: how to approach it, how to handle it, when and why it's dangerous and when it's tame, the meaning of its various cries, and which sounds from another soothe it and which enrage it. Suppose that, by attending on it constantly, he became perfect at all this, and called his knowledge wisdom, and made of it a system and an art he could teach—though he hasn't the faintest real notion which of the creature's moods and desires is honorable or shameful, good or bad, just or unjust. He simply applies the words as the great beast's tastes dictate, calling "good" whatever delights it and "bad" whatever it dislikes, with no other account to give—he calls the necessary "just" and "noble," never having seen, and being unable to show anyone else, how vast the real difference is between necessity and goodness. Heaven help us—wouldn't a man like that be a strange sort of teacher?'
'He certainly would.'

'And how does he differ from the man who thinks wisdom is just knowing the moods and tastes of the mixed-up multitude—in painting, say, or music, or, in the end, in politics? For when a man goes among the many and shows off his poem or some other work of art, or some service he's done the city, and makes them his judges when he isn't forced to, then the "necessity of Diomede," as they call it, will compel him to produce whatever they happen to praise. And yet the reasons they give to back up their notions of what's noble and good are utterly absurd. Have you ever heard one that wasn't?'
'No, and I don't expect to.'

'Then keeping all this in mind, recall the earlier question: will the world ever be brought to believe in the existence of beauty itself, rather than the many beautiful things—of each thing in itself, rather than the many particulars?'
'Certainly not.'
'So the world can't possibly be a philosopher?'
'Impossible.'
'And so philosophers are bound to be condemned by the world?'
'They are.'
'And condemned, too, by the private individuals who keep company with the mob and try to please it?'
'Obviously.'
'Then do you see any way the philosopher can be kept safe in his calling to the end? Remember what we said about him—that he was to have quickness, memory, courage, and greatness of mind.'
'Yes.'
'Won't a man like that, from his earliest childhood, be first among them all in everything—especially if his body matches his mind?'
'He certainly will,' he said.
'And as he grows older, his friends and fellow citizens will want to use him for their own purposes?'
'No question.'
'They'll fall at his feet, begging favors, heaping him with honors and flattery, trying to lay hold in advance of the power that will one day be his.'
'That often happens,' he said.

'And what is a man like that likely to do under these conditions—especially if he's a citizen of a great city, rich and well-born, and a tall, handsome youth? Won't he be filled with boundless ambition, fancying himself fit to manage the affairs of Greeks and barbarians alike, swelling up and giving himself airs, full of empty pomp and senseless pride?'
'He's bound to.'

'Now, while he's in that frame of mind, suppose someone comes to him quietly and tells him the truth—that he has no sense and badly needs it, and that it can only be won by working like a slave for it. Do you think, against such odds, he'll find it easy to listen?'
'Far from it.'

'And even if, through some inborn goodness and natural good sense, one such young man has his eyes opened a little, and is humbled, and won over by philosophy—how will his friends behave when they think they're about to lose the use they hoped to make of him? Won't they do and say anything to keep him from giving in to his better nature, and to make his teacher powerless—plotting against him in private and prosecuting him in the courts?'
'There's no doubt of it.'
'And how can a man in that position ever become a philosopher?'
'He can't.'

'Then weren't we right to say that the very qualities that make a man a philosopher can, if he's badly brought up, turn him away from philosophy just as much as wealth and everything that goes with it and the other so-called goods of life?'
'We were quite right.'

'So this, my excellent friend, is the whole story of how the natures best suited to the best of all pursuits are ruined and lost—natures we say are rare to begin with. And it's out of this very class that the men come who do the greatest harm to cities and to individuals—and the greatest good, too, when the current carries them that way. A small nature never did anything great, for an individual or a city.'
'Very true,' he said.

'And so philosophy is left forsaken, her marriage rite unfinished. Her own kin have fallen away and abandoned her, and while they live their false and unbecoming lives, other men, unworthy of her, see that she has no relatives to protect her, and move in and dishonor her—and fasten on her the very reproaches her critics throw at her, that her followers are some of them good for nothing and most of them deserve the harshest punishment.'
'That's certainly what people say.'

'And what else would you expect,' I said, 'when you think of the puny little men who, seeing this field open before them—a field full of grand names and impressive titles—come bolting into philosophy like convicts breaking out of prison and dashing into a temple? They jump straight out of their trades into philosophy, and the ones who do are usually the cleverest at their own shabby crafts. For even in her present sorry state, philosophy keeps a dignity that the other arts don't have, and many a man is drawn to her whose nature is stunted, whose soul is as cramped and disfigured by his mean little trade as his body is. Isn't that bound to happen?'
'Yes.'

'Aren't they exactly like a bald little tinker who's come into some money, just out of prison, freshly bathed and in a new coat, all dressed up like a bridegroom to marry his master's daughter, now that the family has fallen on poverty and ruin?'
'A perfect parallel.'
'And what will the offspring of such marriages be—won't they be base and bastard?'
'There's no question of it.'

'And when men unworthy of education come up to philosophy and make an alliance with her, who is so far above them, what kind of ideas and opinions are they likely to produce? Won't they be sophisms that flatter the ear, with nothing genuine in them, nothing worthy of true wisdom or akin to it?'
'No doubt,' he said.

'So then, Adeimantus,' I said, 'the worthy followers of philosophy will be only a small remnant. Maybe some noble, well-bred soul kept by exile from the corrupting influences, who stays loyal to her; or some lofty mind born in a small city, whose politics he looks down on and ignores; or a gifted few who leave behind the crafts they rightly despise and come to her. And perhaps a few are held back by the bridle that held our friend Theages: everything in his life conspired to drag him away from philosophy, but bad health kept him out of politics and so kept him in it. My own case—the inner sign that holds me back—is hardly worth mentioning, since such a guide has rarely if ever been given to anyone else. Now those who belong to this small class have tasted how sweet and blessed a thing it is to possess philosophy, and they've also seen clearly enough the madness of the crowd. They've seen that hardly anyone in public life acts honestly, and that there's no ally at whose side a man might fight for justice and come through alive. Such a man is like someone fallen among wild beasts: he won't join in their wrongdoing, but he can't hold out alone against all of them in their savagery, and so, seeing that he'd be no use to the city or to his friends and would only throw his life away without helping anyone, he keeps quiet and goes his own way. He's like a man caught in a driving storm of dust and hail who takes shelter behind a wall. Watching the rest of mankind brimming with lawlessness, he's content if only he can keep his own life clean of injustice and unholy deeds, and at the end depart in peace and good will, with bright hopes.'
'Well,' he said, 'that's no small thing for him to have done before he goes.'
'No small thing,' I said, 'but not the greatest, unless he finds a city that suits him. In a city that suits him, he'll grow to his full stature and save his country along with himself.'
'The reasons philosophy is so badly spoken of have now been explained well enough,' I said, 'and the injustice of the charges against her has been shown. Is there anything more you'd like to add?'
'Nothing more on that,' he replied, 'but I'd like to know which of the existing forms of government you think suits her.'

'None of them,' I said. 'And that's exactly my complaint against them: not one is worthy of the philosophic nature, and so that nature gets warped and changed. Just as foreign seed sown in alien ground loses its character and is overpowered and absorbed into the new soil, so this growth of philosophy, instead of keeping its own strength, degenerates into something else. But if philosophy ever finds the perfection that matches her own in a city, then it will be clear that she is truly divine, and that everything else—all human natures and institutions—is merely human. And now, I know, you're going to ask me what that city is.'
'No,' he said, 'there you're wrong. I wasn't going to ask that. I was going to ask whether you mean the city we ourselves founded, or some other.'

'Ours,' I replied, 'in most respects—though you may remember I said before that there would always have to be some living authority in the city, holding the same conception of the constitution that guided you when, as legislator, you laid down the laws.'
'That was said,' he replied.
'Yes, but not as fully as it should have been. You scared us off by raising objections that showed the discussion would be long and hard—and what's left is the hardest part of all.'
'What's left?'
'The question of how a city can take up the study of philosophy without destroying itself. Every great venture is risky—"hard is the good," as the saying goes.'
'Still,' he said, 'let's get this cleared up, and then the inquiry will be complete.'

'It won't be any lack of will that stops me,' I said, 'but, if anything, a lack of power. You'll see my eagerness for yourselves. Notice, now, how boldly and without hesitation I say that cities ought to take up philosophy—not the way they do now, but in a completely different spirit.'
'In what way?'

'As things stand,' I said, 'the people who study philosophy are very young—boys barely past childhood—and they give it only the scraps of time left over from money-making and managing a household, and then they drop it, just when they come up against the hardest part of the subject, dialectic, even those reputed to have the most philosophic spirit. Later in life, if someone else invites them, they may go and hear a lecture, and they make a great fuss about it, since they don't regard philosophy as their proper business. And in the end, when they grow old, in most cases their philosophic fire is snuffed out—snuffed out more completely than Heraclitus' sun, since it never lights up again.'
'And what should their course be instead?' he asked.

'Just the opposite. In childhood and youth they should be given the study and the philosophy suited to their age. While they're growing toward manhood, the chief care should go to the body, so they'll have it ready for the service of philosophy. Then, as life goes on and the mind begins to mature, they should step up the exercise of the soul. And when their strength fails and they're past the duties of citizen and soldier, then let them range freely and take on no serious labor, since we mean them to live happily here and to crown this life with a like happiness in the next.'

'How truly in earnest you are, Socrates!' he said. 'I'm sure of it. And yet I think most of your hearers will be even more in earnest in opposing you, and will never be convinced—Thrasymachus least of all.'

'Don't start a quarrel between me and Thrasymachus,' I said. 'We've just become friends—though in fact we were never enemies. I'll keep at it with all my strength until I either win him and other men over, or at least do something to profit them against the day when they're born again and have a conversation like this one in another life.'
'You're talking about a time that's not exactly close at hand.'

'Rather,' I replied, 'about a time that's nothing at all compared with eternity. Still, I'm not surprised the many don't believe it, since they've never seen what we're talking about come true. They've only seen an artificial imitation of philosophy, words strung together by design, not, like ours, having a natural unity. A human being who, in word and deed, is shaped as perfectly as a man can be into the proportion and likeness of virtue, and who rules a city built in the same image—that they've never seen, not one such man, and not many. Do you think they ever have?'
'No, never.'

'No, my friend, and they've rarely if ever even heard free and noble talk—the kind of talk men use when they're seeking the truth with all their power, for the sake of knowing, while they hold themselves coldly aloof from the clever wrangling whose only aim is reputation and victory, whether they run into it in the courts or in private company.'
'They're strangers to such talk,' he said.

'And this is exactly what we foresaw, and why the truth forced us to admit, not without fear and hesitation, that no city, no state, and no individual will ever reach perfection until the small class of philosophers we called useless but not corrupt are compelled by some providence, willing or not, to take charge of the city, and the city is compelled to obey them—or until kings, or the sons of kings and rulers, are seized by some divine inspiration with a true love of true philosophy. I see no reason to claim that either of these is impossible. If they were, we'd deserve to be laughed at as dreamers and idle visionaries. Am I not right?'
'Quite right.'

'Then if ever, in the endless ages of the past, or now in some distant land far beyond our knowledge, or someday in the future, the perfect philosopher has been or will be compelled by a higher power to take charge of a city, we're ready to argue to the death that our constitution has existed, and does exist, and will exist whenever this Muse of Philosophy is mistress of a city. There's nothing impossible in it. That it's difficult, we ourselves admit.'
'I agree,' he said.
'But are you going to tell me that the multitude don't think so?'
'I imagine not,' he replied.

'My friend,' I said, 'don't be so hard on the multitude. They'll change their minds if, instead of attacking them, you gently set out to soothe them and to clear away their prejudice against the love of learning. Show them the philosophers as they really are, describe their nature and their calling as you were just now doing, and people will see that the man you're talking about isn't the creature they imagined. Looked at in this new light, surely they'll change their opinion of him and answer in a different tone. Who could be at war with a man who shows him no ill will, who's himself gentle and free of envy—who'd be jealous of one who has no jealousy in him? Let me answer for you: in a few you may find this harsh temper, but not in the majority of mankind.'
'I quite agree,' he said.

'And don't you think too, as I do, that the harsh feeling the many have toward philosophy comes from the pretenders—the ones who barge in uninvited, forever abusing one another, finding fault, and making people, rather than ideas, the subject of their talk? Nothing could be more unbecoming in a philosopher than that.'
'Nothing could be more unbecoming.'

'For the man whose mind is truly fixed on being, Adeimantus, has no time to look down at the petty affairs of men, or to fill himself with malice and envy by fighting with them. His gaze is always on things fixed and unchanging, things that neither wrong one another nor are wronged, but stand in order, all moving according to reason; these he imitates, and to these he makes himself as like as he can. Can a man help imitating that with which he keeps reverent company?'
'Impossible.'
'And so the philosopher, keeping company with the divine and orderly, becomes orderly and divine himself, as far as a man can—though, like everyone else, he'll have his slanderers.'
'Of course.'

'And if he were forced to take what he sees up there and work it into the characters of men, both in their public and their private lives, instead of just shaping himself, do you think he'd be a poor craftsman of temperance and justice and all civic virtue?'
'Anything but poor.'

'And if people come to see that what we're saying about him is true, will they still be angry with philosophy? Will they refuse to believe us when we tell them no city can be happy unless its plan is drawn by artists working from the divine pattern?'
'They won't be angry, if they understand,' he said. 'But how exactly will these men draw out the plan you speak of?'

'They'll start by taking the city and the characters of its people as their canvas, and the first thing they'll do is wipe it clean. That's no easy task. But here, easy or not, is where they'll differ from every other lawgiver: they won't touch an individual or a city, or write a single law, until they've either found a clean surface or made one themselves.'
'And they'll be right to,' he said.
'Once they've done that, won't they sketch the outline of the constitution?'
'No doubt.'

'And then, as they fill in the picture, I imagine they'll keep glancing back and forth—looking, on the one side, at justice itself, beauty itself, temperance, and the rest, and on the other at the human copy they're shaping—blending and tempering the various elements of life into the image of a man, guided by that other image which, when it appears in human beings, Homer too called godlike and the likeness of God.'
'Very true,' he said.
'And they'll rub out one feature and paint in another, until they've made human characters as dear to God as human characters can be?'
'They could make no fairer picture than that,' he said.

'And now,' I said, 'are we beginning to win over the men you described as charging at us full force? Are we persuading them that the painter of constitutions is just the sort of man we've been praising—the one they were so furious at us for putting in charge of the city—and are they growing a little calmer now that they've heard this?'
'Much calmer,' he said, 'if they have any sense.'
'Why, what ground for objection could they still have? Will they doubt that the philosopher is a lover of truth and being?'
'They couldn't be so unreasonable.'
'Or that his nature, as we've drawn it, is akin to the highest good?'
'They can't doubt that either.'
'Or will they say that such a nature, set in favorable conditions, won't turn out perfectly good and wise, if any nature ever could? Will they prefer the men we rejected?'
'Surely not.'
'Then will they still be angry when we say that until philosophers rule, neither cities nor individuals will have any rest from evil, and this city of ours in words will never be realized?'
'I think they'll be less angry.'
'Shall we say, then, that they're not just less angry but completely won over—that they've come around, and out of shame, if nothing else, can't refuse to make peace?'
'By all means,' he said.
'Then suppose the reconciliation is made. Will anyone deny the other point—that there could be sons of kings or rulers who are philosophers by nature?'
'Surely no one,' he said.

'And once such men are born, will anyone insist that they must necessarily be corrupted? That they're hard to save, even we don't deny—but that in the whole course of the ages not one of them could ever escape—who would dare to claim that?'
'Who indeed!'
'But one is enough,' I said. 'Let there be a single such man, with a city ready to obey him, and he could bring into being the whole ideal state the world finds so hard to believe in.'
'Yes, one is enough.'
'For if the ruler lays down the laws and institutions we've described, surely the citizens might be willing to carry them out?'
'Certainly.'
'And it's no miracle, no impossibility, that others should approve of what we approve?'
'I think not.'
'And we've shown well enough already, in what came before, that all this, if only it's possible, is also for the best.'
'We have.'
'So now we can say not only that our laws would be best if they could be enacted, but also that enacting them, though hard, is not impossible.'
'Very good.'

'And so, after all this labor, we've come to the end of one subject. But there's more to discuss: how, and by what studies and pursuits, are the saviors of our constitution to be produced, and at what ages are they to take up their various studies?'
'Yes, there is.'

'I dodged the troublesome business of how the women are to be shared, and the begetting of children, and the choosing of rulers, because I knew the whole arrangement would be looked at with envy and was hard to bring about. But that bit of cleverness did me little good, since I've had to discuss them all the same. The women and children are settled now, but the question of the rulers we'll have to take up again from the very beginning. We said, if you remember, that they had to be lovers of their country, tested by pleasures and pains, and that in no hardship, no danger, no critical moment must they ever let their loyalty slip—whoever failed was to be rejected, and whoever came through pure, like gold tried in the fire, was to be made a ruler and given honors and rewards both in life and after death. That was the sort of thing we were saying, when the argument turned aside and veiled her face, not wanting to stir up the very question that has now come up.'
'I remember perfectly,' he said.
'Yes, my friend,' I said, 'I shrank then from saying the bold word. But now let me dare to say it: the perfect guardian must be a philosopher.'
'Yes,' he said, 'let that be settled.'
'And don't imagine there will be many of them. The gifts we decided were essential rarely grow together in one nature; they usually come in scattered bits and pieces.'
'How do you mean?' he asked.

'You know that quickness of mind, good memory, shrewdness, cleverness, and the like don't often grow together, and that the people who have them, and who are also spirited and high-minded, aren't by nature inclined to live in an orderly, calm, and settled way. Their impulses carry them every which way, and all steadiness deserts them.'
'Very true,' he said.

'On the other hand, the steady, dependable natures, the ones who can't be moved by fear in battle and hold their ground, are just as immovable when it comes to learning. They're sluggish, always half-asleep, yawning their way through any intellectual effort.'
'Quite true.'
'And yet we said both sets of qualities were needed in the men who are to get the higher education and to share in any office or command.'
'Certainly,' he said.
'And won't such men be rare?'
'Very rare indeed.'

'Then the candidate must be tested not only in the labors, dangers, and pleasures we mentioned before, but in another way we didn't mention—he must be exercised in many kinds of knowledge too, to see whether his soul can endure the highest of all studies, or whether it will flinch from them, the way some men flinch from other trials.'
'Yes,' he said, 'you're quite right to test him. But what do you mean by the highest of all knowledge?'
'You'll remember,' I said, 'that we divided the soul into three parts, and from that worked out the natures of justice, temperance, courage, and wisdom?'
'If I'd forgotten that,' he said, 'I wouldn't deserve to hear any more.'
'And do you remember the warning that came before that discussion?'
'What warning?'

'We said, if I'm not mistaken, that to see those virtues in their full beauty a man would have to take a longer way around, at the end of which they'd come clear, but that we could tack on a popular account of them, on the level of the discussion that had gone before. And you said that account would do for you—and so the inquiry went on in what seemed to me a very imprecise way. Whether it satisfied you is for you to say.'
'It did,' he said. 'I thought, and so did the others, that you gave us a fair measure of truth.'

'But, my friend,' I said, 'a measure of such things that falls short, even a little, of the whole truth is no fair measure. Nothing incomplete is the measure of anything—though people are often content with it, and think they needn't look any further.'
'That's a common thing,' he said, 'when people are lazy.'
'Yes,' I said, 'and it's the very last fault that should be allowed in a guardian of the city and its laws.'
'True.'

'Then the guardian must be made to take the longer way around, and to work as hard at learning as at physical training—or he'll never reach the highest knowledge of all, which, as we've just said, is his proper concern.'
'What,' he said, 'is there a knowledge still higher than this—higher than justice and the other virtues?'

'There is,' I said. 'And even with the virtues, we mustn't be satisfied with the outline we have now—nothing less than the most finished picture should content us. Isn't it absurd that when small things are worked out with endless pains so they'll appear in their full clarity and beauty, we should think the highest truths don't deserve the highest precision?'
'A fine thought,' he said. 'But do you suppose we'll let you off without asking what this highest knowledge is, and what it's about?'

'Ask, by all means,' I said. 'Though I'm sure you've heard the answer many times, and now either you don't follow me or, as I rather think, you mean to make trouble for me. For you've often been told that the Form of the Good is the highest object of knowledge, and that it's by their relation to it that just things and the rest become useful and beneficial. You can hardly be unaware that this is what I was about to speak of—the thing we know so little about, as you've often heard me say, and without which any other knowledge or possession does us no good at all. Do you think there's any value in possessing everything else, if we don't possess the good? Or in knowing everything else, with no knowledge of the beautiful and the good?'
'Certainly not.'
'And you know, too, that most people say the good is pleasure, while the more sophisticated say it's knowledge?'
'Yes.'
'And that the ones who say knowledge can't tell us what knowledge they mean, but are forced in the end to say "knowledge of the good"?'
'How absurd!'

'Yes,' I said—'first they reproach us with not knowing the good, and then they turn around and talk to us as though we did, since they define the good as knowledge of the good, as if we understood them when they say the word "good." That, of course, is ridiculous.'
'It certainly is,' he said.
'And those who define the good as pleasure are in just as much of a tangle, since they're forced to admit there are bad pleasures as well as good ones.'
'Certainly.'
'And so to admit that the same things are both good and bad?'
'True.'
'There's no doubt this question is wrapped in difficulties.'
'None at all.'

'And don't we see this too: that with the just and the honorable, many people are happy to seem to have them, or to be thought to do them, even without the reality—but with the good, no one is content with the mere appearance. Everyone wants the real thing; here, appearance is despised by all?'
'Very true,' he said.

'This, then—which every soul pursues and for the sake of which it does all that it does, sensing somehow that there is such a thing, yet baffled, never quite able to grasp its nature or to feel about it the steady confidence it has about other things, and so losing whatever good there might be in those other things—this, of all things, is what the best men in our city, the men to whom everything is entrusted, must not be left to grope after in the dark. Should they be?'
'Certainly not,' he said.
'I'm sure,' I said, 'that a man who doesn't know how the beautiful and the just are also good will make a poor guardian of them. And I suspect no one will truly know them until he knows the good.'
'That,' he said, 'is a shrewd guess.'
'And if we have a guardian who has this knowledge, our city will be perfectly ordered?'
'Of course,' he replied. 'But I wish you'd tell me—do you think this supreme good is knowledge, or pleasure, or something else again?'
'There you are,' I said. 'I knew all along that a fastidious man like you would never be content with other people's opinions about these things.'
'It doesn't seem right, Socrates,' he said, 'for a man who's spent his whole life on philosophy to keep repeating other people's views and never give his own.'
'Well,' I said, 'has anyone the right to speak with confidence about what he doesn't know?'
'He has no right,' he said, 'to speak as though he were certain. But he may say what he thinks, as a matter of opinion.'

'And don't you know,' I said, 'that opinions cut off from knowledge are all worthless, and the best of them blind? You wouldn't deny that people who hold some true notion without understanding are like blind men who happen to be on the right road?'
'Very true.'
'And do you really want to gaze at what's blind and crooked and dim, when you can hear from others about what's bright and beautiful?'

'For heaven's sake, Socrates,' Glaucon said, 'don't quit just as you're reaching the finish line. We'll be satisfied if you'll give us an account of the good like the one you gave of justice and temperance and the other virtues.'

'And I'd be just as satisfied myself, my friend,' I said. 'But I'm afraid I'll fall short, and that my clumsy eagerness will make me look foolish. So, gentlemen, let's set aside for now the question of what the good actually is. To reach what I have in mind about it would be too great an effort for me as I am. But I'm willing to tell you about the child of the good, the thing most like it—if you'd care to hear it. If not, we'll leave it.'
'Tell us about the child, by all means,' he said. 'You can still owe us the account of the parent another time.'

'I only wish,' I replied, 'that I could pay that debt now, and you collect it—the account of the parent and not just of the offspring. Take this one, then, as interest in the meantime. But be on your guard that I don't cheat you with a false account of the interest, even though I've no intention of deceiving you.'
'We'll be as careful as we can,' he said. 'Go on.'
'I will,' I said, 'but first let me reach an understanding with you, and remind you of something I've said in the course of this discussion and on many other occasions too.'
'What's that?'
'The old point that there are many beautiful things and many good things, each of which we describe and define as such, applying the word "many" to them.'
'True,' he said.
'And that there is also beauty itself and good itself, and so for all the things we called "many"—for each set of them can be gathered under a single Form, which we call what each really is.'
'Very true.'
'And we say the many are seen but not known, while the Forms are known but not seen.'
'Exactly.'
'Now, with what part of ourselves do we see the things that are seen?'
'With our sight,' he said.
'And with our hearing we hear, and with the other senses perceive everything else that's perceived?'
'True.'
'But have you noticed,' I said, 'that the craftsman who fashioned the senses made the power of sight and being seen by far the most lavish and complex of them all?'
'No, I never noticed that,' he said.

'Then think about it this way. Do hearing and sound need any third thing, so that the one may hear and the other be heard—some extra nature, without which the one won't hear and the other won't be heard?'
'Nothing of the kind.'
'No,' I said—'and the same is true of most of the other senses, if not all. You wouldn't say any of them needs such an addition?'
'No, I wouldn't.'
'But don't you notice that sight and the things seen do need exactly that—some additional nature?'
'How do you mean?'

'Suppose sight is in the eyes, and the man who has it is trying to use it, and color is present in the things—still, unless there's a third thing, of a kind made specially for the purpose, you know that the eyes will see nothing, and the colors will stay invisible.'
'What is this thing you're talking about?' he asked.
'What you call light,' I replied.
'True,' he said.
'So no small thing links sight and the power to be seen—a bond more precious by far than any that ties the other senses to their objects, since light is no mean thing.'
'No,' he said, 'light is far from a mean thing.'
'And which of the gods in heaven would you name as the lord of this light, the one whose light makes our sight see, and makes visible things appear?'
'The same one you and everyone names,' he said. 'You mean the sun.'
'And isn't this how sight stands in relation to that god?'
'How?'
'Neither sight itself, nor the eye in which it lives, is the sun.'
'No.'
'But of all the organs of sense, the eye is surely the most sunlike?'
'By far the most.'
'And the power the eye has, it draws as a kind of overflow from the sun's store?'
'Exactly.'
'So the sun is not itself sight, but it's the cause of sight and is seen by the very sight it causes?'
'True,' he said.

'Well, this is what I meant by the child of the good—the one the good begot in its own likeness. What the good is in the intelligible world, in relation to intelligence and the things known, the sun is in the visible world, in relation to sight and the things seen.'
'Will you explain that a little more?' he said.

'You know,' I said, 'that when the eyes are turned toward things no longer lit by daylight, but only by the moon and stars, they see dimly and are nearly blind, as though there were no clear sight in them.'
'Very true.'
'But when they're turned toward things the sun shines on, they see clearly, and the same eyes plainly have sight in them.'
'Certainly.'

'It's the same with the soul. When it fixes itself on what truth and being shine upon, it understands and knows it and is plainly full of intelligence. But when it turns toward what is mixed with darkness, toward what comes to be and passes away, then it only has opinions, and it grows dim, shifting its opinions back and forth, and seems to have no intelligence at all.'
'Just so.'

'Now, what gives truth to the things known, and the power of knowing to the one who knows, is what I want you to call the Form of the Good. Think of it as the cause of knowledge and of truth, in so far as truth is known. Beautiful as both knowledge and truth are, you'll be right to regard the good as different from them, and more beautiful still. And just as in the other case it was right to call light and sight sunlike, but not to call them the sun, so here it's right to call knowledge and truth good-like, but wrong to call either of them the good. The good holds a place of honor higher still.'
'You're speaking of an extraordinary beauty,' he said, 'if it produces knowledge and truth and yet surpasses them in beauty. You surely don't mean that it's pleasure?'
'Heaven forbid,' I replied. 'But let me press the image a little further.'
'In what way?'

'You'd say, wouldn't you, that the sun gives visible things not only the power of being seen, but also their coming-to-be, their growth, and their nourishment—though the sun is not itself a coming-to-be?'
'Of course.'

'In the same way, you should say that the things we know not only get their being known from the good, but also their very being and existence, while the good is not itself existence, but lies even beyond existence, surpassing it in dignity and power.'
And here Glaucon said, with a comic earnestness, 'Good lord! What a staggering height!'
'You brought it on yourself,' I said. 'You're the one who made me say what I think.'
'And don't stop now,' he said. 'Go on—at least finish telling us about the likeness to the sun, if there's anything more.'
'There's a great deal more,' I said.
'Then leave nothing out, however small.'
'I'll do my best,' I said, 'though I think a great deal will have to be left out.'
'I hope not,' he said.

'Picture, then, two ruling powers, one set over the intelligible world and the other over the visible—I won't say "the heavens," or you'll think I'm playing on the words. So you have these two before your mind, the visible and the intelligible?'
'I do.'

'Now take a line cut into two unequal parts. Then cut each part again in the same ratio—one part standing for the visible world, the other for the intelligible—and compare the sections by their clearness and dimness. The first section in the visible world will be images. By images I mean, first, shadows, and then reflections in water and on smooth, polished surfaces, and everything of that sort. Do you follow?'
'I follow.'
'Now let the second section stand for the things the first section was an image of—the animals around us, and every growing thing, and everything made by hand.'
'Very good.'
'And would you agree that these two sections differ in their degree of truth, and that the copy stands to the original as the realm of opinion stands to the realm of knowledge?'
'Most certainly.'
'Now consider how the intelligible part of the line is to be divided.'
'How?'

'Like this. In the lower of its two sections, the soul uses as images the very things that were originals before—the things in the visible world—and is forced to work from assumptions, not traveling up toward a first principle but down toward a conclusion. In the higher section, the soul moves from an assumption up toward a principle that needs no assumption, and it makes no use of images, as it did below, but works through the Forms themselves and by means of them alone.'
'I don't quite follow you,' he said.

'Then let me try again,' I said. 'You'll understand me better after a few preliminary remarks. You know that students of geometry and arithmetic and the kindred sciences take for granted the odd and the even, the various figures, the three kinds of angles, and the like, each in their own branch. They treat these as assumptions, as things everyone already knows, and so they don't think they owe any account of them, to themselves or anyone else, but start from them and go on, step by consistent step, to the conclusion they set out to reach.'
'Yes,' he said, 'I know that.'

'And you also know that, although they use visible figures and reason about them, they aren't really thinking about those figures, but about the things the figures resemble. They reason about the square itself and the diagonal itself, not the particular square they've drawn; the figures they draw or model—which themselves cast shadows and reflections in water—they now treat in turn as mere images, while they're really trying to see the things themselves, which can be seen only by thought.'
'That's true.'

'This, then, is the kind of thing I called intelligible—but with the qualification that, in studying it, the soul is forced to use assumptions, and doesn't travel up to a first principle, since it can't rise above its assumptions. It uses as images the very things below, the things of which the shadows are themselves resemblances—things that, compared with their shadows and reflections, count as clear and are valued accordingly.'
